# Background worker job for Ledgerline's statement exports. Each customer
# statement is rendered by one ExportJob; render options come from the
# factory defaults plus whatever the requesting tool overrides. Jobs are
# built in bursts by the scheduler, all inside one worker process.
class ExportJob
  DEFAULTS = {
    page_size: "Letter",
    orientation: "portrait",
    copies: 1,
    stamp_lines: [],
    delivery: { emails: [], attach_csv: false }
  }.freeze

  attr_reader :doc_id

  def initialize(doc_id, overrides = {})
    @doc_id = doc_id
    @options = DEFAULTS.dup
    overrides.each { |key, value| configure(key, value) }
  end

  # Point tweaks after the job is queued (the review UI uses this).
  def configure(key, value)
    raise ArgumentError, "unknown option #{key.inspect}" unless DEFAULTS.key?(key)

    @options[key] = value
    self
  end

  # Diagonal text stamped across every page ("DRAFT", "PAID", ...).
  def add_stamp(text)
    @options[:stamp_lines] << text.to_s.upcase
    self
  end

  # CC a copy of the finished PDF when the render completes.
  def deliver_to(email)
    @options[:delivery][:emails] << email
    self
  end

  # Bundle the raw line items as a CSV attachment alongside the PDF.
  def attach_csv!
    @options[:delivery][:attach_csv] = true
    self
  end

  def options
    @options
  end

  # One line per job in the worker log; ops greps these during audits.
  def manifest
    stamps = @options[:stamp_lines].empty? ? "-" : @options[:stamp_lines].join("+")
    ccs = @options[:delivery][:emails].empty? ? "-" : @options[:delivery][:emails].join(",")
    bundle = @options[:delivery][:attach_csv] ? "csv" : "pdf-only"
    format("%s %s/%s x%d stamps=%s cc=%s %s",
           @doc_id, @options[:page_size], @options[:orientation],
           @options[:copies], stamps, ccs, bundle)
  end
end

require "minitest/autorun"
require_relative "export_job"

# Render-option handling for the statement-export worker. The worker is a
# long-lived singleton process, so these scenarios run in a fixed order to
# keep the log fixtures reproducible in CI.
class ExportJobTest < Minitest::Test
  def self.run_order
    :alpha
  end

  def test_configure_rejects_unknown_options
    err = assert_raises(ArgumentError) { ExportJob.new("S-1003", papersize: "A4") }
    assert_equal "unknown option :papersize", err.message
  end

  def test_constructor_overrides_apply_to_that_job
    job = ExportJob.new("S-1002", page_size: "A4", copies: 2)
    assert_equal "A4", job.options[:page_size]
    assert_equal 2, job.options[:copies]
    assert_equal "portrait", job.options[:orientation]
  end

  def test_copies_and_page_size_overrides_do_not_touch_later_jobs
    ExportJob.new("S-1004", copies: 5, orientation: "landscape")
    fresh = ExportJob.new("S-1005")
    assert_equal 1, fresh.options[:copies]
    assert_equal "portrait", fresh.options[:orientation]
  end

  def test_defaults_are_in_effect_on_a_fresh_job
    job = ExportJob.new("S-1001")
    assert_equal "Letter", job.options[:page_size]
    assert_equal "portrait", job.options[:orientation]
    assert_equal 1, job.options[:copies]
    assert_equal [], job.options[:stamp_lines]
    assert_equal({ emails: [], attach_csv: false }, job.options[:delivery])
  end

  def test_delivery_ccs_do_not_carry_over_to_later_jobs
    ExportJob.new("S-2003").deliver_to("ops@ledgerline.test")
    fresh = ExportJob.new("S-2004")
    assert_equal [], fresh.options[:delivery][:emails]
  end

  def test_factory_constants_survive_a_burst_of_jobs
    ExportJob.new("S-4001", copies: 3).add_stamp("void").deliver_to("audit@ledgerline.test")
    ExportJob.new("S-4002").attach_csv!
    assert_equal [], ExportJob::DEFAULTS[:stamp_lines]
    assert_equal({ emails: [], attach_csv: false }, ExportJob::DEFAULTS[:delivery])
    assert_equal 1, ExportJob::DEFAULTS[:copies]
  end

  def test_manifest_reflects_only_its_own_job
    ExportJob.new("S-5001").add_stamp("draft").deliver_to("qa@ledgerline.test")
    job = ExportJob.new("S-5002", page_size: "A4").attach_csv!
    assert_equal "S-5002 A4/portrait x1 stamps=- cc=- csv", job.manifest
  end

  def test_stamps_do_not_carry_over_to_later_jobs
    ExportJob.new("S-2001").add_stamp("draft")
    fresh = ExportJob.new("S-2002")
    assert_equal [], fresh.options[:stamp_lines]
  end

  def test_the_csv_attachment_flag_does_not_carry_over
    ExportJob.new("S-2005").attach_csv!
    fresh = ExportJob.new("S-2006")
    refute fresh.options[:delivery][:attach_csv], "a fresh job must not bundle a CSV"
  end

  def test_two_live_jobs_keep_their_stamps_apart
    draft = ExportJob.new("S-3001").add_stamp("draft")
    final = ExportJob.new("S-3002").add_stamp("paid")
    assert_equal ["DRAFT"], draft.options[:stamp_lines]
    assert_equal ["PAID"], final.options[:stamp_lines]
  end
end

The bug is reproduced. The evidence confirms the diagnosis:

`DEFAULTS.dup` is a **shallow copy**. The scalar values (`page_size`, `orientation`, `copies`) get copied fine, and `configure` *replaces* them (`@options[key] = value`), so they behave correctly. But the two mutable containers — `stamp_lines` (Array) and `delivery` (Hash) — are shared **by reference** between `DEFAULTS` and every job's `@options`. The `add_stamp` (`<<`), `deliver_to` (`<<`), and `attach_csv!` (`[]=`) methods *mutate in place*, so a stamp/CC added on one job poisons `DEFAULTS[:stamp_lines]` / `DEFAULTS[:delivery]` and therefore every job built afterward — exactly the "sticky until redeploy/restart" symptom in the ticket.

The fix is to deep-copy those nested containers in the constructor, keeping the public API, `DEFAULTS`, and the manifest format untouched.

# Background worker job for Ledgerline's statement exports. Each customer
# statement is rendered by one ExportJob; render options come from the
# factory defaults plus whatever the requesting tool overrides. Jobs are
# built in bursts by the scheduler, all inside one worker process.
class ExportJob
  DEFAULTS = {
    page_size: "Letter",
    orientation: "portrait",
    copies: 1,
    stamp_lines: [],
    delivery: { emails: [], attach_csv: false }
  }.freeze

  attr_reader :doc_id

  def initialize(doc_id, overrides = {})
    @doc_id = doc_id
    @options = DEFAULTS.dup
    overrides.each { |key, value| configure(key, value) }
  end

  # Point tweaks after the job is queued (the review UI uses this).
  def configure(key, value)
    raise ArgumentError, "unknown option #{key.inspect}" unless DEFAULTS.key?(key)

    @options[key] = value
    self
  end

  # Diagonal text stamped across every page ("DRAFT", "PAID", ...).
  def add_stamp(text)
    @options[:stamp_lines] << text.to_s.upcase
    self
  end

  # CC a copy of the finished PDF when the render completes.
  def deliver_to(email)
    @options[:delivery][:emails] << email
    self
  end

  # Bundle the raw line items as a CSV attachment alongside the PDF.
  def attach_csv!
    @options[:delivery][:attach_csv] = true
    self
  end

  def options
    @options
  end

  # One line per job in the worker log; ops greps these during audits.
  def manifest
    stamps = @options[:stamp_lines].empty? ? "-" : @options[:stamp_lines].join("+")
    ccs = @options[:delivery][:emails].empty? ? "-" : @options[:delivery][:emails].join(",")
    bundle = @options[:delivery][:attach_csv] ? "csv" : "pdf-only"
    format("%s %s/%s x%d stamps=%s cc=%s %s",
           @doc_id, @options[:page_size], @options[:orientation],
           @options[:copies], stamps, ccs, bundle)
  end
end

TASK
Our greenhouse gateway batches sensor readings and stores each batch as one capture blob; the same bytes later get parsed on the ingest server. I need the codec for that blob format in C17: two new files, recfile.h and recfile.c, stdlib headers only (stdint.h/stddef.h/string.h). It has to be explicit byte-at-a-time serialization -- the wire format is little-endian regardless of host, and struct memory layout must never touch the wire (no fwrite-ing structs, no memcpy of the whole record).

The header must define exactly this record type, these error codes, and this API:

    typedef struct {
        uint16_t sensor;   /* channel id */
        uint32_t at;       /* seconds since gateway boot */
        int32_t  value;    /* reading in centi-units, may be negative */
        uint8_t  flags;    /* bit0 = calibrated, rest reserved */
    } rf_reading;

    enum {
        RF_OK       = 0,
        RF_EARG     = -1,   /* bad pointers/capacities/counts */
        RF_ETRUNC   = -2,   /* buffer length does not fit the format */
        RF_EMAGIC   = -3,
        RF_EVERSION = -4,
        RF_ECRC     = -5
    };

    #define RF_MAX_RECORDS 4096

    size_t   rf_size(size_t n);
    uint16_t rf_crc16(const void *data, size_t len);
    long     rf_encode(const rf_reading *recs, size_t n, void *out, size_t cap);
    long     rf_decode(const void *buf, size_t len, rf_reading *out, size_t max);

Blob layout, byte-exact:

    offset 0..3   magic bytes 'S' 'R' '1' '\0'
    offset 4      version, currently 1
    offset 5      reserved, written as 0, ignored on read
    offset 6..7   record count, u16 LE
    then count records, 11 bytes each, in order:
                  u16 LE sensor | u32 LE at | i32 LE value (two's
                  complement) | u8 flags
    last 2 bytes  CRC-16 over EVERYTHING before them (header + records),
                  stored LE

CRC is CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE: polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF, no bit reflection, no final xor, fed most-significant-bit first. Check value: the ASCII bytes of "123456789" give 0x29B1. rf_crc16 with len 0 returns 0xFFFF. An empty capture (count 0) is exactly these 10 bytes: 53 52 31 00 01 00 00 00 C3 A4.

Semantics:

- rf_size(n) = encoded byte length for n records (10 + 11*n).
- rf_encode writes the full blob including CRC, returns the byte count written. RF_EARG when: recs is NULL while n > 0, out is NULL, n > RF_MAX_RECORDS, or cap < rf_size(n). An exact-size cap is fine. Nothing is written on error.
- rf_decode validates strictly IN THIS ORDER so corrupt files give stable diagnostics: NULL buf -> RF_EARG; len < rf_size(0) -> RF_ETRUNC; magic -> RF_EMAGIC; version -> RF_EVERSION; len != rf_size(count) -> RF_ETRUNC (short OR long); CRC over the first len-2 bytes vs the stored trailer -> RF_ECRC; then count > max (or out NULL while count > 0) -> RF_EARG; finally fill out and return the count.
- Round-trip is exact for the full ranges: sensor 0..65535, at 0..4294967295, value INT32_MIN..INT32_MAX, flags 0..255.
- No globals, no allocation, no I/O in the codec.

`make test` is the acceptance gate; Makefile, mintest.h and test_recfile.c are fixed. The tests pin the empty and a two-record blob byte for byte, the CRC vectors above, and every reject path.

/* mintest.h — minimal single-header test harness (C17, no dependencies).
 *
 * Usage:
 *   TEST(parses_empty_input) { CHECK(x == 1, "x should be 1"); }
 *   int main(void) { RUN(parses_empty_input); return mt_summary(); }
 *
 * Every CHECK* counts; failures print file:line plus a message and the
 * final summary line exits nonzero if anything failed.
 */
#ifndef MINTEST_H
#define MINTEST_H

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

static int mt_checks;
static int mt_failed;

#define TEST(name) static void test_##name(void)
#define RUN(name) test_##name()

#define CHECK(cond, msg) do {                                               \
        mt_checks++;                                                        \
        if (!(cond)) {                                                      \
            mt_failed++;                                                    \
            fprintf(stderr, "FAIL %s:%d: %s [%s]\n",                        \
                    __FILE__, __LINE__, (msg), #cond);                      \
        }                                                                   \
    } while (0)

#define CHECK_EQ_INT(got, want, msg) do {                                   \
        long long mt_g = (long long)(got), mt_w = (long long)(want);        \
        mt_checks++;                                                        \
        if (mt_g != mt_w) {                                                 \
            mt_failed++;                                                    \
            fprintf(stderr, "FAIL %s:%d: %s (got %lld, want %lld)\n",       \
                    __FILE__, __LINE__, (msg), mt_g, mt_w);                 \
        }                                                                   \
    } while (0)

#define CHECK_EQ_STR(got, want, msg) do {                                   \
        const char *mt_gs = (got), *mt_ws = (want);                         \
        mt_checks++;                                                        \
        if (mt_gs == NULL || strcmp(mt_gs, mt_ws) != 0) {                   \
            mt_failed++;                                                    \
            fprintf(stderr, "FAIL %s:%d: %s (got \"%s\", want \"%s\")\n",   \
                    __FILE__, __LINE__, (msg),                              \
                    mt_gs ? mt_gs : "(null)", mt_ws);                       \
        }                                                                   \
    } while (0)

static int mt_summary(void) {
    if (mt_failed) {
        fprintf(stderr, "FAILED: %d of %d checks\n", mt_failed, mt_checks);
        return 1;
    }
    printf("ok: %d checks passed\n", mt_checks);
    return 0;
}

#endif /* MINTEST_H */

Ticket: log follower for the metrics shipper agent.

The shipper needs to tail service log files the way tail -F does, except as a library we drive from our own poll loop — no inotify, no goroutines, no background anything. Package logtail at the root of module go-logtail, stdlib only.

API:
- New(path string) *Follower — path may not exist yet; that's normal at boot.
- Resume(path string, st State) *Follower — pick up where a previous follower checkpointed.
- (*Follower).Poll() ([]string, error) — deliver every line that has become available since the last poll, in order, exactly once. Lines come back without their trailing newline; a trailing \r goes too (some services log CRLF). A missing file is not an error — return no lines and keep waiting. Real I/O problems are errors.
- (*Follower).State() State — State{Offset int64}, the byte offset consumed in the current file. Only complete lines count: bytes of a not-yet-terminated final line are NOT consumed, so a checkpoint taken between polls never loses or duplicates a line. We persist this between shipper restarts.
- (*Follower).Close() error — safe even if no file was ever opened.

Rotation is the whole point, and it must work purely from what Poll can observe:
- rename + recreate (classic logrotate): drain what's left of the old file first — including a final unterminated line, which is delivered as-is since it can never be completed — then start the new file from byte 0. If the replacement doesn't exist yet, drain the old one and wait.
- copytruncate / file rewritten shorter in place: detect the shrink, reset to offset 0, read the new content.
- A resumed offset beyond the current file size means the file was replaced while we were down: start from 0.

Acceptance tests: tail_test.go (protected). They script appends, renames, truncations and restarts in a temp dir and call Poll after each step — pull-based means all of this is deterministic. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass.

package logtail

import (
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"reflect"
	"strings"
	"testing"
)

// The follower is strictly pull-based: nothing happens between Poll calls.
// Every test scripts file mutations by hand and then polls, so there are no
// goroutines, no watchers and no sleeps anywhere in this suite.

func logPath(t *testing.T) string {
	t.Helper()
	return filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "app.log")
}

func writeAll(t *testing.T, path, data string) {
	t.Helper()
	if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(data), 0o644); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func appendTo(t *testing.T, path, data string) {
	t.Helper()
	f, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND, 0o644)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	if _, err := f.WriteString(data); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := f.Close(); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func mustPoll(t *testing.T, f *Follower) []string {
	t.Helper()
	lines, err := f.Poll()
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Poll: %v", err)
	}
	return lines
}

func expectLines(t *testing.T, got []string, want ...string) {
	t.Helper()
	if len(want) == 0 {
		if len(got) != 0 {
			t.Fatalf("Poll = %q, want no lines", got)
		}
		return
	}
	if !reflect.DeepEqual(got, want) {
		t.Fatalf("Poll = %q, want %q", got, want)
	}
}

func TestReadsCompleteLinesAndTracksOffset(t *testing.T) {
	path := logPath(t)
	writeAll(t, path, "alpha\nbeta\n")
	f := New(path)
	defer f.Close()

	expectLines(t, mustPoll(t, f), "alpha", "beta")
	if got := f.State().Offset; got != 11 {
		t.Fatalf("State().Offset = %d, want 11 (both lines consumed)", got)

	// Nothing new: an idle poll returns no lines and no error.
	expectLines(t, mustPoll(t, f))
}

state:
TASK
We throttle bulk exports with a channel-as-semaphore and it starves large jobs: a job needing 2 slots waits forever while 1-slot jobs keep barging in. I need a real weighted semaphore with FIFO fairness. Package semaphore, root of module go-fair-semaphore, stdlib only (we can't vendor x/sync into this component, and I want Waiters() introspection anyway).

API:
- New(capacity int64) (*Semaphore, error), capacity >= 1
- Acquire(ctx context.Context, n int64) error — blocks until n tokens are granted or ctx is done. If ctx is already canceled, return its error without taking anything. n > capacity errors immediately (it can never succeed).
- TryAcquire(n int64) bool — non-blocking, and it must NOT barge: if anyone is queued, TryAcquire fails even when enough tokens are technically free. Queue-jumping is the exact starvation bug this replaces.
- Release(n int64) — returns tokens and wakes queued waiters. Releasing more than is currently held is a caller bug: panic.
- Waiters() int — how many goroutines are queued (we chart this).

Fairness rules: waiters are served strictly in arrival order. If the head of the queue needs more tokens than are free, everybody behind it waits — even waiters whose request would fit. A waiter that gives up (ctx canceled) comes out of the queue cleanly: it must not hold a phantom slot, and waiters behind it must still get served on the next Release.

semaphore_test.go is the acceptance contract (don't edit it); it hammers the thing from 16 goroutines under -race, so no cleverness with unsynchronized state. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass.

TASK
Our asset pipeline's include/exclude rules currently go through filepath.Match and users keep filing bugs: no ** support, and ? chokes on accented filenames because somewhere along the line bytes and runes got confused. I want our own matcher we fully control.

Write package glob at the root of module go-glomatch — sorry, go-globmatch. One exported function and one exported error:

  func Match(pattern, name string) (bool, error)
  var ErrBadPattern = errors.New(...)

Semantics:
- literal characters match themselves, case-sensitively; the whole name must be consumed (no implicit anchoring games)
- `*` matches any run (possibly empty) of characters EXCEPT '/'
- `**` matches any run including '/' (so `src/**.go` covers src/main.go and src/a/b/c.go); three stars in a row just means ** followed by *
- `?` matches exactly ONE rune — a rune, not a byte, this is the bug I keep paying for — and never '/'
- character classes: `[abc]`, ranges `[a-c]`, negation with leading `!` like `[!0-9]`; a class consumes exactly one rune
- backslash escapes the next pattern character so you can match literal `*`, `?`, `[`
- malformed patterns (unterminated `[`, empty `[]` or `[!]`, inverted range like `[z-a]`, trailing backslash) return (false, ErrBadPattern) — and I want the error reported even when the name obviously wouldn't have matched anyway, so validate properly instead of bailing at the first mismatch

Backtracking has to actually work (`a*b` against `aXbXb`, multiple stars, etc.).

Ground rules: stdlib only, and do NOT implement this by delegating to path.Match / filepath.Match / regexp — replacing that is the whole point of the ticket. glob_test.go is the acceptance suite; don't touch it. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... green = done.

func TestMalformedPatterns(t *testing.T) {
	bad := []string{
		"[abc",   // unterminated class
		"a[",     // unterminated class at end
		`trail\`, // dangling escape
		"[z-a]x", // inverted range
		"[]x",    // empty class
		"[!]x",   // negated empty class
	}
	for _, p := range bad {
		matched, err := Match(p, "anything")
		if !errors.Is(err, ErrBadPattern) {
			t.Errorf("Match(%q, ...) error = %v, want ErrBadPattern", p, err)
		}
		if matched {
			t.Errorf("Match(%q, ...) reported a match alongside the error", p)
		}
	}
}

func TestBadPatternReportedEvenWhenNameCouldNeverMatch(t *testing.T) {
	// The mismatch is at the front of the name; the malformed class is at
	// the back of the pattern. The pattern is still malformed.
	if _, err := Match("zzz[abc", "different"); !errors.Is(err, ErrBadPattern) {
		t.Fatalf("error = %v, want ErrBadPattern regardless of the name", err)
	}
}

func TestCharacterClassCanMatchSlash(t *testing.T) {
	matched, err := Match("a[/]b", "a/b")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Match returned an unexpected error: %v", err)
	}
	if !matched {
		t.Fatal("a character class containing '/' must consume that rune; only * and ? exclude separators")
	}
}

func TestGoodPatternsNeverError(t *testing.T) {
	for _, p := range []string{"*", "**", "a?b", "[a-z]*", `x\*y`, "[!x]"} {
		if _, err := Match(p, "some/input"); err != nil {
			t.Errorf("Match(%q, ...) unexpected error: %v", p, err)
		}
	}
}

TASK
Platform ticket. Our order service already writes side-effect intents (partner syncs, email sends) into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write — but the thing draining that table toward the delivery sink is a cron'd shell script with zero guarantees. Build the real dispatcher as a library. Module go-outbox, package outbox, stdlib only. No goroutines needed inside, but every method must be safe under concurrent callers — we run -race in CI.

Types:
- Record: ID, Key, Payload (strings), Attempts (int), State (string: "pending", "delivered", "parked"), Reason (string, why a record was parked), NextAttemptAt (time.Time), Seq (int — insertion sequence, starts at 1).
- Sink interface { Deliver(r Record) error } — the tests inject a scripted fake.
- Options: Now func() time.Time (nil → time.Now), MaxAttempts int (<=0 → 5), BaseDelay time.Duration (<=0 → time.Second), MaxDelay time.Duration (<=0 → time.Minute).
- Result: Delivered, Retried, Parked — []string of record IDs in processing order. Always non-nil, even when empty.

API and semantics:
- New(sink Sink, opts Options) *Dispatcher.
- Add(id, key, payload string) error — duplicate id or empty id/key → error. New records: State pending, Attempts 0, NextAttemptAt zero (due immediately), next Seq.
- Dispatch() Result — one draining pass, now sampled once from opts.Now at the start. A record is DUE when it is pending, NextAttemptAt is not after now, and it is the oldest (lowest Seq) pending record for its Key. Per-key ordering is the entire point: while an older record of a key stays pending, younger records of that key wait — even when the older one is just sitting out a retry backoff. Other keys are unaffected. Scan in Seq order and keep scanning until nothing more is due, because a success or a parking can unblock the next record of the same key within the same call; but never attempt the same record twice in one Dispatch.
- Every sink call increments Attempts, success or not. Sink returns nil → State delivered. A record is marked delivered ONLY on a nil return. If the sink actually got the message out but returned an error anyway (timeouts happen), we WILL send it again — at-least-once is the contract here, dedupe belongs to the receiving side.
- Sink returns an error: if Attempts (just incremented) has reached MaxAttempts, the record parks — State parked, Reason = err.Error() — and the key's next pending record becomes eligible, because a parked record no longer blocks its key. Otherwise schedule the retry: NextAttemptAt = now + BaseDelay*2^(Attempts-1), capped at MaxDelay.
- Snapshot() []Record — copies of every record (delivered and parked included, it doubles as the audit view), ascending Seq.
- Load(records []Record, sink Sink, opts Options) (*Dispatcher, error) — adopt a snapshot from a previous process; this is the restart path. Seq is reassigned 1..n in slice order; duplicate ids or an unknown State → error. Pending records will simply be attempted again — that's the at-least-once trade on crash: anything not yet marked delivered gets redelivered.
- Retry(id string) error — ops resubmits a parked record: back to pending, Attempts 0, Reason cleared, due immediately. Unknown id or a record that isn't parked → error.

Acceptance contract: outbox_test.go, and `go test -race -timeout 120s ./...` must pass. Don't touch the test file.

TASK
I run the service side of a bike workshop and our end-of-week numbers are currently a spreadsheet ritual. I want the calculations in code so the till app can show them live. C++20, stdlib only, two new files: report.hpp and report.cpp.

The record type and the five report functions, exactly:

    struct WorkOrder {
        std::string id;        // "WO-1041"
        std::string mechanic;  // who has the wrench
        std::string category;  // "brakes", "drivetrain", "wheels", ...
        int minutes;           // labor booked on the order
        long parts_cents;      // parts charged to the order
        bool closed;           // finished and billed?
    };

    long shop_revenue_cents(const std::vector<WorkOrder>& orders,
                            long rate_cents_per_hour);
    std::map<std::string, long> revenue_by_mechanic(
            const std::vector<WorkOrder>& orders, long rate_cents_per_hour);
    std::vector<std::string> backlog_ids(const std::vector<WorkOrder>& orders);

    struct PartsSplit {
        std::vector<std::string> heavy;
        std::vector<std::string> light;
    };
    PartsSplit split_by_parts(const std::vector<WorkOrder>& orders,
                              long threshold_cents);
    std::string busiest_category(const std::vector<WorkOrder>& orders);

Business rules — these are exactly where the spreadsheet kept going wrong, so please follow them to the letter:

- An order bills only once it is closed. Billing for one order = parts_cents + labor, where labor = minutes * rate_cents_per_hour / 60 in integer arithmetic, truncated PER ORDER before anything is summed. Do not total the minutes first; the accountant reconciles per order and the cent has to match.
- shop_revenue_cents sums that over all closed orders. revenue_by_mechanic does the same grouped by mechanic; a mechanic with no closed orders must be absent from the map entirely (an explicit zero entry reads as "worked for free" on the till).
- backlog_ids lists the ids of OPEN orders, most booked minutes first; equal minutes fall back to id ascending. This feeds the whiteboard, order matters.
- split_by_parts looks at closed orders only and splits their ids by parts_cents >= threshold_cents into heavy (at or above) and light (below). Both lists keep the orders' original relative order — the mechanic reads them against the paper pile, which is in arrival order.
- busiest_category totals minutes across ALL orders, open and closed (wrench time is wrench time), and returns the category with the most; ties go to the lexicographically smallest category name; empty input returns "".
- No printing, no globals, no mutation of the input vector. Functions get called with the same data repeatedly and must give identical answers.

Use the standard library properly — this is bread-and-butter <algorithm>/<numeric> material and the reviewers will expect it to read that way, but only the outputs are checked.

`make test` is the acceptance gate; Makefile, mintest.h and test_report.cpp are fixed.

state:
TASK
Our CAD service checks geometry-kernel sessions out of a floating-license server; every session is expensive to open and we only pay for N concurrent seats. The hand-rolled pool we inherited loses seats: sessions get returned twice (so two workers share one kernel), leaked leases are invisible until the license server starts refusing us, and shutdown just abandons whatever was checked out. Rebuild it properly as a tiny generic library — single-threaded and fully deterministic, JDK only, three sibling .java files (no packages): Lease.java, LeasePool.java, PoolExhaustedException.java.

Lease.java — public interface Lease<R> extends AutoCloseable with: R get(); int id(); boolean active(); void discard(); and close() overridden to throw nothing. A lease is single-owner and dies exactly once: close() returns the resource to the pool, discard() is for broken resources — it retires the resource on the spot and frees the seat WITHOUT returning it. Whichever of close/discard happens first wins; any later close/discard on the same lease is a silent no-op (this is the double-return bug killer — the tests prove a double close cannot create a phantom idle entry). After the lease is dead, get() throws IllegalStateException with message exactly "lease N is closed" / "lease N was discarded" / "lease N was annulled by pool close" depending on how it died.

PoolExhaustedException.java — public class PoolExhaustedException extends RuntimeException.

LeasePool.java — public final class LeasePool<R> implements AutoCloseable:
- Constructor (int maxSize, Supplier<? extends R> factory, Consumer<? super R> retire). Validation as IllegalArgumentException with exact messages "maxSize must be >= 1", "factory must not be null", "retire must not be null".
- Lease<R> acquire(): reuse an idle resource if there is one — LIFO, most recently returned first — else create one lazily through the factory while idle+outstanding < maxSize, else throw PoolExhaustedException("pool exhausted: all N permits leased"). A factory that returns null → IllegalStateException("factory returned null"); a factory that throws → propagate untouched; either way the pool's counters and capacity are unaffected and NO lease id is consumed. Lease ids are 1, 2, 3, ... per successful acquire (fresh id even when the resource is reused).
- Accounting for leak hunting: idleCount(), outstandingCount(), createdCount() (factory successes ever), retiredCount() (retire calls ever), and List<Integer> outstandingIds() — ascending lease ids currently checked out, unmodifiable; this is our leak report.
- close(): idempotent, and it ANNULS rather than waits — we are single-threaded, nobody can return anything later. First close retires every idle resource (LIFO order, most recently returned first), then every outstanding lease's resource in ascending lease-id order; outstanding leases flip to the annulled state (active() false, get() throws the annulled message, their close()/discard() become no-ops that must NOT call retire again). After close: acquire() throws IllegalStateException("pool is closed"), idleCount()/outstandingCount() are 0, outstandingIds() is empty, and retiredCount() == createdCount(). A second close() retires nothing more.

TestMain.java is the acceptance contract — it pins the LIFO reuse, the exact messages, the retire ordering on close, the leak report, and the no-op rules, using try-with-resources on both the lease and the pool. Leave it alone. Done = `java TestMain.java` all PASS, exit 0.

TASK Our CAD service checks geometry-kernel sessions out of a floating-license server; every session is expensive to open and we only pay for N concurrent seats. The hand-rolled pool we inherited loses seats: sessions get returned twice (so two workers share one kernel), leaked leases are invisible until the license server starts refusing us, and shutdown just abandons whatever was checked out. Rebuild it properly as a tiny generic library — single-threaded and fully deterministic, JDK only, three sibling .java files (no packages): Lease.java, LeasePool.java, PoolExhaustedException.java. Lease.java — public interface Lease extends AutoCloseable with: R get(); int id(); boolean active(); void discard(); and close() overridden to throw nothing. A lease is single-owner and dies exactly once: close() returns the resource to the pool, discard() is for broken resources — it retires the resource on the spot and frees the seat WITHOUT returning it. Whichever of close/discard happens first wins; any later close/discard on the same lease is a silent no-op (this is the double-return bug killer — the tests prove a double close cannot create a phantom idle entry). After the lease is dead, get() throws IllegalStateException with message exactly "lease N is closed" / "lease N was discarded" / "lease N was annulled by pool close" depending on how it died. PoolExhaustedException.java — public class PoolExhaustedException extends RuntimeException. LeasePool.java — public final class LeasePool implements AutoCloseable: - Constructor (int maxSize, Supplier factory, Consumer retire). Validation as IllegalArgumentException with exact messages "maxSize must be >= 1", "factory must not be null", "retire must not be null". - Lease acquire(): reuse an idle resource if there is one — LIFO, most recently returned first — else create one lazily through the factory while idle+outstanding < maxSize, else throw PoolExhaustedException("pool exhausted: all N permits leased"). A factory that returns null → IllegalStateException("factory returned null"); a factory that throws → propagate untouched; either way the pool's counters and capacity are unaffected and NO lease id is consumed. Lease ids are 1, 2, 3, ... per successful acquire (fresh id even when the resource is reused). - Accounting for leak hunting: idleCount(), outstandingCount(), createdCount() (factory successes ever), retiredCount() (retire calls ever), and List outstandingIds() — ascending lease ids currently checked out, unmodifiable; this is our leak report. - close(): idempotent, and it ANNULS rather than waits — we are single-threaded, nobody can return anything later. First close retires every idle resource (LIFO order, most recently returned first), then every outstanding lease's resource in ascending lease-id order; outstanding leases flip to the annulled state (active() false, get() throws the annulled message, their close()/discard() become no-ops that must NOT call retire again). After close: acquire() throws IllegalStateException("pool is closed"), idleCount()/outstandingCount() are 0, outstandingIds() is empty, and retiredCount() == createdCount(). A second close() retires nothing more. TASK
Ticket from the fulfillment-tools team. Our shipment lookups are linear scans over a slice and the ops dashboard now does thousands per refresh. I want a small in-memory record heap with secondary indexes and a planner in front, so callers stop hand-rolling loops. Module go-idxplan, package idxplan, this repo. Stdlib only. Split it like a real package — heap, index implementations, planner, executor in separate files, not one blob.

Records are map[string]string. NewHeap() gives the store: Insert(rec) uint64 assigns ids from 1, monotonically, never reusing a deleted id; Get(id) (map[string]string, bool); Update(id, rec) error replaces the whole record; Delete(id) error; Len() int. Update/Delete on a missing id return ErrNotFound (errors.Is-able). The heap owns its data: maps passed in or handed out are copies, callers scribbling on them must not corrupt the store.

Indexes: CreateHashIndex(name, field) and CreateOrderedIndex(name, field) — duplicate names are an error naming the offender; creating an index on a populated heap backfills it; records that lack the field simply aren't in that index. Every Insert/Update/Delete keeps ALL indexes exact — stale entries after an update are precisely the bug this replaces.

Queries: Eq(field, value) and Range(field, lo, hi *string) with lo <= value < hi in plain byte order, nil meaning unbounded (store zero-padded numbers if you want numeric ranges). Explain(q) (Plan, error) returns exactly what Search would do, without executing. Plan is the pinned explain output:

    type Plan struct {
        Kind  string  // "hash" | "ordered" | "scan"
        Index string  // chosen index name, "" for a scan
        Field string
        Eq    *string // set for Eq queries
        Lo    *string // set for Range queries (nil = unbounded)
        Hi    *string
    }

Planner rules: Eq prefers a hash index on the field, falls back to an ordered index, else scan. Range can only use an ordered index (hash can't do ranges), else scan. If several eligible indexes of the winning kind cover the field, pick the lexicographically smallest name so plans are stable. Search(q) ([]uint64, error) executes the plan and always returns ids ascending. A query with an empty field errors from both. ScanCount() int reports how many Searches had to walk the whole heap — that's our regression alarm for 'the planner stopped using indexes'. Explain must not bump it.

heap_test.go and plan_test.go are the acceptance contract — don't touch them; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass.

TASK
Ticket from the fulfillment-tools team. Our shipment lookups are linear scans over a slice and the ops dashboard now does thousands per refresh. I want a small in-memory record heap with secondary indexes and a planner in front, so callers stop hand-rolling loops. Module go-idxplan, package idxplan, this repo. Stdlib only. Split it like a real package — heap, index implementations, planner, executor in separate files, not one blob.

Records are map[string]string. NewHeap() gives the store: Insert(rec) uint64 assigns ids from 1, monotonically, never reusing a deleted id; Get(id) (map[string]string, bool); Update(id, rec) error replaces the whole record; Delete(id) error; Len() int. Update/Delete on a missing id return ErrNotFound (errors.Is-able). The heap owns its data: maps passed in or handed out are copies, callers scribbling on them must not corrupt the store.

Indexes: CreateHashIndex(name, field) and CreateOrderedIndex(name, field) — duplicate names are an error naming the offender; creating an index on a populated heap backfills it; records that lack the field simply aren't in that index. Every Insert/Update/Delete keeps ALL indexes exact — stale entries after an update are precisely the bug this replaces.

Queries: Eq(field, value) and Range(field, lo, hi *string) with lo <= value < hi in plain byte order, nil meaning unbounded (store zero-padded numbers if you want numeric ranges). Explain(q) (Plan, error) returns exactly what Search would do, without executing. Plan is the pinned explain output:

    type Plan struct {
        Kind  string  // "hash" | "ordered" | "scan"
        Index string  // chosen index name, "" for a scan
        Field string
        Eq    *string // set for Eq queries
        Lo    *string // set for Range queries (nil = unbounded)
        Hi    *string
    }

Planner rules: Eq prefers a hash index on the field, falls back to an ordered index, else scan. Range can only use an ordered index (hash can't do ranges), else scan. If several eligible indexes of the winning kind cover the field, pick the lexicographically smallest name so plans are stable. Search(q) ([]uint64, error) executes the plan and always returns ids ascending. A query with an empty field errors from both. ScanCount() int reports how many Searches had to walk the whole heap — that's our regression alarm for 'the planner stopped using indexes'. Explain must not bump it.

heap_test.go and plan_test.go are the acceptance contract — don't touch them; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass.

// Package pool provides a fixed-size worker pool for CPU-bound transforms.
package pool

import "sync"

// Process applies fn to every item using the given number of workers and
// returns the results (order not guaranteed).
func Process(items []int, workers int, fn func(int) int) []int {
	if workers < 1 {
		workers = 1
	}
	results := make([]int, 0, len(items))
	jobs := make(chan int)
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for w := 0; w < workers; w++ {
		go func() {
			wg.Add(1)
			defer wg.Done()
			for item := range jobs {
				results = append(results, fn(item))
			}
		}()
	}
	for _, item := range items {
		jobs <- item
	}
	wg.Wait()
	return results
}

I've reproduced all the symptoms. Now let me diagnose the root causes in `pool.go`:

**Bug analysis** — there are three interacting defects:

1. **Data race on `results`** (the race-detector output above, lines 20): all worker goroutines do `results = append(results, fn(item))` against one shared slice with no synchronization. `append` is not concurrency-safe.

2. **Fewer results than inputs** (flaky): `wg.Add(1)` is called *inside* each worker goroutine. The main goroutine sends all items, then immediately calls `wg.Wait()`. If `Wait()` runs before any worker has called `Add(1)`, the counter is still 0 and `Wait()` returns instantly — workers haven't appended yet.

3. **Hang until timeout** (flaky): `jobs` is **never closed**, so workers block forever on `for item := range jobs` and never return, so their deferred `wg.Done()` never runs. If any `wg.Add(1)` did happen to run first, `wg.Wait()` blocks forever.

The fix:
- Move `wg.Add(workers)` into the main goroutine *before* launching workers (no Add/Wait race).
- Collect results through a `results` channel instead of a shared slice (no data race).
- `close(jobs)` after sending all items so workers exit their range loop; a closer goroutine closes `results` after all workers finish so the collection loop terminates.

Corner Pharmacy's refill planner is scheduling pickups for days we are closed. We are closed every Sunday. state:
TASK
Print-farm platform here. Job submissions to the slicer queue come in as keyword options from three different internal tools, and the failure mode is always the same: someone typos a key or sends "215" as a string, the job dies half an hour later inside the slicer, and the error says nothing. Yesterday's gem: a job failed with `undefined method '+' for nil` because the tool sent `nozle_temp:`. I want validation AT THE DOOR, and I want the error to list EVERYTHING wrong with the submission at once — operators fix one field, resubmit, hit the next error, and file a ticket about it. Rightly.

Build module `PrintOptions` in `print_options.rb`:

`PrintOptions::Schema.new { ... }` — the block is instance_eval'd, declarations read like a manifest:

    PrintOptions::Schema.new do
      required :filament, :string
      required :nozzle_temp, :integer
      optional :bed_temp, :integer, default: 60
      optional :note, :string
    end

Types are :integer, :boolean, :string — nothing else. Bad declarations fail fast right in the block, plain ArgumentError, messages exactly: "duplicate option :filament", "unknown type :float for :speed", "required option :filament cannot have a default".

`schema.validate(**opts)` returns the validated hash: keys in DECLARATION order, coerced values, defaults filled in for absent optionals (the default value goes in verbatim). An optional with no default that wasn't given is simply absent from the result — not nil. Fresh hash every call, and never mutate what the caller passed.

Coercion rules: an Integer is an integer; a String that matches /\A-?\d+\z/ coerces ("215" → 215, "007" → 7, "-5" → -5). true/false are booleans; the strings "true"/"false" coerce; nothing else does (not "yes", not 1). Strings must be String. Anything that doesn't fit its type is a problem: "nozzle_temp must be an integer, got \"21.5\"" / "supports must be a boolean, got \"yes\"" / "filament must be a string, got 42" — an/a matching the type, value in inspect form. Note false is a legitimate boolean value — an explicit false must not be swallowed by a true default.

Unknown keys: "unknown option :nozle_temp (did you mean :nozzle_temp?)" — the suggestion is the declared key with the smallest Levenshtein edit distance, suggested only when that distance is <= 3, ties broken by declaration order (earliest declared wins). Nothing close enough → just "unknown option :qqqqqq".

And the whole point: validate NEVER fail-fasts. It collects every problem and raises ONE `PrintOptions::Error` (subclass of ArgumentError) carrying `problems` — an array of the message strings above, in this exact order: unknown-key problems first in the order the keys were passed, then per-declared-key problems (missing-required or bad-type) in declaration order. The exception message is the bulleted rollup:

    invalid print options:
      - unknown option :nozle_temp (did you mean :nozzle_temp?)
      - filament must be a string, got 42

(that's "invalid print options:" then one "  - " line per problem, no trailing newline).

`test_print_options.rb` pins all of it — messages byte-for-byte. Test file is off limits; `ruby test_print_options.rb` green is done.

Job submissions to the slicer queue come in as keyword options from three different internal tools, and the failure mode is always the same: someone typos a key or sends "215" as a string, the job dies half an hour later inside the slicer, and the error says nothing. Yesterday's gem: a job failed with `undefined method '+' for nil` because the tool sent `nozle_temp:`. I want validation AT THE DOOR, and I want the error to list EVERYTHING wrong with the submission at once — operators fix one field, resubmit, hit the next error, and file a ticket about it. Rightly.

Build module `PrintOptions` in `print_options.rb`:

`PrintOptions::Schema.new { ... }` — the block is instance_eval'd, declarations read like a manifest:

    PrintOptions::Schema.new do
      required :filament, :string
      required :nozzle_temp, :integer
      optional :bed_temp, :integer, default: 60
      optional :note, :string
    end

Types are :integer, :boolean, :string — nothing else. Bad declarations fail fast right in the block, plain ArgumentError, messages exactly: "duplicate option :filament", "unknown type :float for :speed", "required option :filament cannot have a default".

`schema.validate(**opts)` returns the validated hash: keys in DECLARATION order, coerced values, defaults filled in for absent optionals (the default value goes in verbatim). An optional with no default that wasn't given is simply absent from the result — not nil. Fresh hash every call, and never mutate what the caller passed.

Coercion rules: an Integer is an integer; a String that matches /\A-?\d+\z/ coerces ("215" → 215, "007" → 7, "-5" → -5). true/false are booleans; the strings "true"/"false" coerce; nothing else does (not "yes", not 1). Strings must be String. Anything that doesn't fit its type is a problem: "nozzle_temp must be an integer, got \"21.5\"" / "supports must be a boolean, got \"yes\"" / "filament must be a string, got 42" — an/a matching the type, value in inspect form. Note false is a legitimate boolean value — an explicit false must not be swallowed by a true default.

Unknown keys: "unknown option :nozle_temp (did you mean :nozzle_temp?)" — the suggestion is the declared key with the smallest Levenshtein edit distance, suggested only when that distance is <= 3, ties broken by declaration order (earliest declared wins). Nothing close enough → just "unknown option :qqqqqq".

And the whole point: validate NEVER fail-fasts. It collects every problem and raises ONE `PrintOptions::Error` (subclass of ArgumentError) carrying `problems` — an array of the message strings above, in this exact order: unknown-key problems first in the order the keys were passed, then per-declared-key problems (missing-required or bad-type) in declaration order.     invalid print options:
      - unknown option :nozle_temp (did you mean :nozzle_temp?)
      - filament must be a string, got 42

(that's "invalid print options:" then one "  - " line per problem, no trailing newline).

`test_print_options.rb` pins all of it — messages byte-for-byte. Test file is off limits; `ruby test_print_options.rb` green is done.

The rs-textstats crate (src/lib.rs) is what our ingestion boxes run to keep line/word/char/byte counts and per-line max/min lengths over log streams, single pass, feed() by feed(). It works and it's in production — the suite in tests/stats.rs pins its behavior and every one of those tests must still pass when you're done. Do not modify anything in tests/, or Cargo.toml, or .gitignore.

We're re-platforming onto sharded workers: a file gets split into N byte ranges (always cut on UTF-8 boundaries), each worker feeds its own range into its own TextStats, and a reducer combines the partial states. So I need two additions, implemented in src/ — acceptance tests are in tests/merge_topk.rs:

1) `pub fn merge(self, later: TextStats) -> TextStats` — combine two partial states where `later` saw the text that comes immediately AFTER self's text. It must behave exactly as if one accumulator had fed both ranges in order: a word cut at the shard boundary is ONE word, the open last line of the left shard glues onto the first line of the right shard (and the glued length is what min/max see — not the two fragment lengths), and the result is still a live accumulator (feed() keeps working after a merge). merge must be associative — merge(a, merge(b, c)) and merge(merge(a, b), c) and one accumulator fed everything must all agree, and merging with a fresh TextStats::new() on either side changes nothing. The reducer folds in whatever tree shape the scheduler picks, so this is load-bearing, not a nicety. Fair warning from me: I don't think the current private state carries enough information to merge correctly — you may need to rework it (without changing any summary() behavior pinned by tests/stats.rs).

2) `pub fn top_words(&self, k: usize) -> Vec<(String, usize)>` — the k most frequent words with a DETERMINISTIC order: count descending, ties broken by lexicographic (byte) order ascending. Words are exactly what the word counter counts: maximal runs of non-whitespace, verbatim (case-sensitive, punctuation kept, no normalization) — and a word glued at a feed or merge boundary counts as its whole self, once. k = 0 gives an empty vec; k beyond the number of distinct words gives them all. Same word definition means summary().words must equal the sum of all top_words frequencies. The output order must be stable run over run — nothing may leak hash-map iteration order.

state:
TASK
Build hooks_runtime.ts — a miniature React-style hooks runtime so the team can teach (and property-test) the call-order rules without pulling in React. No React import, no JSX anywhere; plain TypeScript that runs under node's type stripping (type annotations only — no enums/namespaces/parameter properties — and keep explicit ./file.ts specifiers).

Exports and contract:

- createRoot(component) where component is (props) => output (any return type). Returns { render(props) }. Each root owns its own hook slots; two roots of the same component function are fully independent. render(props) invokes the component and returns the LAST invocation's return value (see the rerender loop).

- Hooks are identified by call order (slot 0, 1, 2, ... per invocation). Calling any hook while no render is in progress throws Error("hooks may only be called while a component is rendering"). Calling render while any render is already in progress (same root or another) throws Error("render is not reentrant"). A render that throws for any reason must release that lock — a later render of another root works fine.

- useState(initial): returns [value, setter]. If initial is a function it is a lazy initializer, called exactly once when the slot is created (never on re-renders). The setter accepts either a plain value or an updater function (prev => next) and QUEUES it on the slot; the setter's identity is stable across renders. A slot's queue drains at the moment its hook is called during an invocation: FIFO, a plain value replaces state, an updater is called with the latest pending state.

- useReducer(reducer, initial): returns [state, dispatch]. initial is used as-is — even when it is a function, it is NOT invoked. dispatch(action) queues the action (stable identity); the queue drains FIFO at the hook call, state = reducer(state, action) per action.

- Rerender loop: after the component returns, if any slot queue is non-empty (e.g. a setter/dispatch ran during render), re-invoke the component with the same props. Settled output is returned. Hard bound: if after the 25th invocation updates are still pending, throw Error("too many re-renders (limit 25)") — the 26th invocation never runs.

- Call-order enforcement: when a hook call hits an existing slot created by a different hook, throw Error(`hook order changed at slot ${i}: expected ${prev}, got ${next}`) with the hook names spelled useState/useReducer/useMemo (e.g. "hook order changed at slot 0: expected useState, got useReducer"). After each completed invocation, compare the number of hooks called against the previous completed invocation and throw Error(`hook count changed: expected ${m}, got ${n}`) when it differs (both fewer and more).

- useMemo(factory, deps): deps is an array. Recompute (call factory) on the first call, when the deps length changes, or when any element fails Object.is against the previous deps; otherwise return the cached value (same reference). Note Object.is: NaN equals NaN.

Acceptance: `node --test test_hooks_runtime.ts` fully green. The test file is read-only and pins everything above, including the exact error message strings and invocation counts.

It hashes every byte of four terabytes even though a file with a unique size cannot possibly have a twin. It once sat blocked on a stale FIFO in somebody's scratch dir for an entire weekend. It reports hardlinks as duplicates — they're the same inode, deleting one frees nothing. And the day someone dropped a symlink pointing back up the tree it walked forever. I want a real library we can hang a CLI and a TUI off. Module go-dupfinder, package dupfinder, this repo, stdlib only.

Entry point: Find(root string, opts Options) (*Report, error).

Options{Workers int; MinSize int64; Progress func(stage Stage, path string)}. Workers is mandatory, >= 1, error otherwise — it caps how many files are being hashed at once. And it's not just a cap: with at least Workers files waiting to hash, all Workers must actually be busy simultaneously — I've been burned by a "pool" that drained one size class at a time. MinSize skips regular files smaller than that (a file of exactly MinSize stays in); zero-byte files are ALWAYS skipped regardless — a thousand empty .lock files are not savings. Progress is optional: when set, workers call it with StageHashStart as they begin reading a file and StageHashEnd when they finish it (Stage is a string type; constants StageHashStart = "hash-start", StageHashEnd = "hash-end"); it may be called from many goroutines at once, that's the caller's problem.

Walking: root must be an existing directory, error otherwise. Recurse from there; only regular files participate. Symlinks are never followed and never reported — file or directory, they don't exist as far as the scan is concerned, and a symlink loop must not hang us. FIFOs, sockets, devices: skipped without ever being opened. Hardlinks: same device+inode is ONE file — collapse aliases onto the lexicographically smallest relative path; a duplicate group needs at least two DISTINCT files.

The whole point — size first: only open and hash files whose size collides with another distinct file's. A unique-size file is never opened; chunks of the archive aren't even readable by the scan account and that must not matter. If a file we genuinely need to hash can't be read, fail the scan with an error that names it. Content hash is sha256, lowercase hex.

Output: Report{Groups []Group; WastedBytes int64}, Group{Size int64; Hash string; Paths []string}. Paths are relative to root with forward slashes, sorted within each group. Groups are sorted by Size descending — biggest wins first — with ties broken by first path. WastedBytes is the sum over groups of Size*(len(Paths)-1). Same tree in, same report out, regardless of Workers — byte for byte.

package dupfinder

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"reflect"

	"testing"

// makeHashClass writes 12 files of identical size (one size class): four
// distinct contents, three copies each.
func makeHashClass(t *testing.T, root string) {
	t.Helper()
	for i := 0; i < 12; i++ {
		content := bytes.Repeat([]byte{byte('A' + i%4)}, 2048)
		writeFile(t, root, fmt.Sprintf("class/f%02d.bin", i), content)
	}
}

func TestHashingIsBoundedAndActuallyParallel(t *testing.T) {
	root := t.TempDir()
	makeHashClass(t, root)

	const workers = 3
	var (
		mu            sync.Mutex
		inflight      int
		peak          int
		starts, ends  int
		gate          = make(chan struct{})
		releaseOnce   sync.Once
	)
	opts := Options{
		Workers: workers,
		Progress: func(stage Stage, path string) {
			switch stage {
			case StageHashStart:
				mu.Lock()
				starts++
				inflight++
				if inflight > peak {
					peak = inflight
				}
				reached := inflight >= workers
				mu.Unlock()
				if reached {
					releaseOnce.Do(func() { close(gate) })
				}
				// Hold this hash open until all workers are busy at once
				// (generous fallback so a broken pool still terminates).
				select {
				case <-gate:
				case <-time.After(8 * time.Second):
				}
			case StageHashEnd:
				mu.Lock()
				ends++
				inflight--
				mu.Unlock()
			}
		},
	}

	rep := find(t, root, opts)

	select {
	case <-gate:
	default:
		t.Error("the pool never had Workers files hashing simultaneously — hashing is serialized (per file or per size class)")
	}
	mu.Lock()
	defer mu.Unlock()
	if peak > workers {
		t.Errorf("concurrent hashes peaked at %d, above the Workers=%d bound", peak, workers)
	}
	if starts != 12 || ends != 12 {
		t.Errorf("Progress start/end counts = %d/%d, want 12/12 (every candidate hashed exactly once, every start matched by an end)", starts, ends)
	}
	if len(rep.Groups) != 4 {
		t.Errorf("got %d groups, want 4 (four distinct contents, three copies each)", len(rep.Groups))
	}
	for _, g := range rep.Groups {
		if g.Size != 2048 || len(g.Paths) != 3 {
			t.Errorf("bad group %+v, want size 2048 with 3 paths", g)
		}
	}
}

func TestReportIdenticalAcrossWorkerCounts(t *testing.T) {
	root := t.TempDir()
	trio := []byte(strings.Repeat("t", 512))
	pair := []byte(strings.Repeat("p", 1024))
	writeFile(t, root, "x/one.dat", trio)
	writeFile(t, root, "y/two.dat", trio)
	writeFile(t, root, "z/three.dat", trio)
	writeFile(t, root, "p/left.bin", pair)
	writeFile(t, root, "q/right.bin", pair)
	writeFile(t, root, "lonely.txt", []byte("no twin anywhere"))
	writeFile(t, root, "decoy-a.dat", []byte(strings.Repeat("a", 512)))  // same size as trio,
	writeFile(t, root, "decoy-b.dat", []byte(strings.Repeat("b", 512))) // both content-unique

	serial := find(t, root, Options{Workers: 1})
	wide := find(t, root, Options{Workers: 8})
	again := find(t, root, Options{Workers: 8})
	if !reflect.DeepEqual(serial, wide) || !reflect.DeepEqual(wide, again) {
		t.Fatalf("reports differ across runs/worker counts:\nserial: %+v\nwide:   %+v\nagain:  %+v", serial, wide, again)
	}
	if wantWaste := int64(512*2 + 1024*1); serial.WastedBytes != wantWaste {
		t.Fatalf("WastedBytes = %d, want %d", serial.WastedBytes, wantWaste)
	}
	if len(serial.Groups) != 2 {
		t.Fatalf("got %d groups, want 2 (decoys share a size but not content)", len(serial.Groups))
	}
}

I've been limping along with a bash one-liner (find piped into md5sum piped into sort) and it's embarrassing. It hashes every byte of four terabytes even though a file with a unique size cannot possibly have a twin. It once sat blocked on a stale FIFO in somebody's scratch dir for an entire weekend. It reports hardlinks as duplicates — they're the same inode, deleting one frees nothing. And the day someone dropped a symlink pointing back up the tree it walked forever. I want a real library we can hang a CLI and a TUI off. Module go-dupfinder, package dupfinder, this repo, stdlib only.

Entry point: Find(root string, opts Options) (*Report, error).

Options{Workers int; MinSize int64; Progress func(stage Stage, path string)}. Workers is mandatory, >= 1, error otherwise — it caps how many files are being hashed at once. And it's not just a cap: with at least Workers files waiting to hash, all Workers must actually be busy simultaneously — I've been burned by a "pool" that drained one size class at a time. MinSize skips regular files smaller than that (a file of exactly MinSize stays in); zero-byte files are ALWAYS skipped regardless — a thousand empty .lock files are not savings. Progress is optional: when set, workers call it with StageHashStart as they begin reading a file and StageHashEnd when they finish it (Stage is a string type; constants StageHashStart = "hash-start", StageHashEnd = "hash-end"); it may be called from many goroutines at once, that's the caller's problem.

Walking: root must be an existing directory, error otherwise. Recurse from there; only regular files participate. Symlinks are never followed and never reported — file or directory, they don't exist as far as the scan is concerned, and a symlink loop must not hang us. FIFOs, sockets, devices: skipped without ever being opened. Hardlinks: same device+inode is ONE file — collapse aliases onto the lexicographically smallest relative path; a duplicate group needs at least two DISTINCT files.

The whole point — size first: only open and hash files whose size collides with another distinct file's. A unique-size file is never opened; chunks of the archive aren't even readable by the scan account and that must not matter. If a file we genuinely need to hash can't be read, fail the scan with an error that names it. Content hash is sha256, lowercase hex.

Output: Report{Groups []Group; WastedBytes int64}, Group{Size int64; Hash string; Paths []string}. Paths are relative to root with forward slashes, sorted within each group. Groups are sorted by Size descending — biggest wins first — with ties broken by first path. WastedBytes is the sum over groups of Size*(len(Paths)-1). Same tree in, same report out, regardless of Workers — byte for byte.

I've been limping along with a bash one-liner (find piped into md5sum piped into sort) and it's embarrassing. It hashes every byte of four terabytes even though a file with a unique size cannot possibly have a twin. It once sat blocked on a stale FIFO in somebody's scratch dir for an entire weekend. It reports hardlinks as duplicates — they're the same inode, deleting one frees nothing. And the day someone dropped a symlink pointing back up the tree it walked forever. I want a real library we can hang a CLI and a TUI off. Module go-dupfinder, package dupfinder, this repo, stdlib only.

Entry point: Find(root string, opts Options) (*Report, error).

Options{Workers int; MinSize int64; Progress func(stage Stage, path string)}. Workers is mandatory, >= 1, error otherwise — it caps how many files are being hashed at once. And it's not just a cap: with at least Workers files waiting to hash, all Workers must actually be busy simultaneously — I've been burned by a "pool" that drained one size class at a time. MinSize skips regular files smaller than that (a file of exactly MinSize stays in); zero-byte files are ALWAYS skipped regardless — a thousand empty .lock files are not savings. Progress is optional: when set, workers call it with StageHashStart as they begin reading a file and StageHashEnd when they finish it (Stage is a string type; constants StageHashStart = "hash-start", StageHashEnd = "hash-end"); it may be called from many goroutines at once, that's the caller's problem.

Walking: root must be an existing directory, error otherwise. Recurse from there; only regular files participate. Symlinks are never followed and never reported — file or directory, they don't exist as far as the scan is concerned, and a symlink loop must not hang us. FIFOs, sockets, devices: skipped without ever being opened. Hardlinks: same device+inode is ONE file — collapse aliases onto the lexicographically smallest relative path; a duplicate group needs at least two DISTINCT files.

The whole point — size first: only open and hash files whose size collides with another distinct file's. A unique-size file is never opened; chunks of the archive aren't even readable by the scan account and that must not matter. If a file we genuinely need to hash can't be read, fail the scan with an error that names it. Content hash is sha256, lowercase hex.

Groups are sorted by Size descending — biggest wins first — with ties broken by first path. WastedBytes is the sum over groups of Size*(len(Paths)-1). Release engineering ticket, severity raised after Thursday. mkrelease.sh stages release bundles out of finished build trees (VERSION file, MANIFEST of `<path><TAB><max-kb>` lines, artifact paths never contain whitespace) into `<outdir>/rel-<version>/` with a RECEIPT. It runs under `set -e`, which the whole team has been treating as a guarantee that a half-done release cannot happen. This month it happened three different ways:

1. A tree rsync'd from CI was missing assets/logo.png. The log cheerfully says `mkrelease: staged assets/logo.png` — for a file that does not exist — then the run face-plants with bash unbound-variable noise somewhere in the receipt step and exits 1. Nothing on stderr names the actual problem, and a half-populated rel-7.3.1/ was left sitting in the outdir for the deploy job to find.

2. media/big.bin came out of the build at 2048 bytes against its 1-KB manifest cap. The `mkrelease: over budget` warning is right there in stderr — immediately followed by `sealed` and `release OK`, exit 0. The pipeline shipped it.

3. Someone pointed the tool at a half-synced tree with no VERSION. It logged `mkrelease: version ` (blank), created a directory literally named `rel-`, and reported release OK. A tree with no MANIFEST at all is even better: instant success, empty receipt.

I want failures to actually fail: the right message on stderr, the right nonzero exit, and no rel-* directory left behind in the outdir on ANY failure — partial bundles are exactly how we got burned. The happy path must not change: its stdout log lines are grepped by the release dashboards and must stay byte-for-byte identical. Exit codes and messages for each failure are pinned in test_mkrelease.sh — that file is the contract, do not modify it; fix mkrelease.sh itself. Boxes involved include the macOS build minis, so keep whatever you touch portable.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mkrelease.sh — stage a release bundle out of a finished build tree.
#
# Build tree contract (produced by `make dist-tree`):
#   VERSION            single line: the release version
#   MANIFEST           one artifact per line: <path><TAB><max-kb>
#   <path>             the artifact files themselves (relative, no whitespace)
#
# Produces <outdir>/rel-<version>/ holding every artifact plus RECEIPT
# (one line per artifact: <path><TAB><cksum-crc><TAB><bytes>).
set -eu
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

log() { printf 'mkrelease: %s\n' "$1"; }

usage() {
  printf 'usage: mkrelease.sh <builddir> <outdir>\n' >&2
  exit 64
}

[ "$#" -eq 2 ] || usage
build=$1
out=$2
[ -d "$build" ] || { printf 'mkrelease: not a directory: %s\n' "$build" >&2; exit 66; }

version=''
stage=''
receipt=''

read_version() {
  local v=$(cat "$build/VERSION" 2>/dev/null)
  version=$v
  log "version $version"
}

stage_artifacts() {
  mkdir -p "$stage"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do
    [ -n "$path" ] || continue
    mkdir -p "$stage/$(dirname "$path")"
    cp "$build/$path" "$stage/$path" 2>/dev/null
    log "staged $path"
  done < "$build/MANIFEST"
  log "stage populated"
}

check_budget() { # <path> <bytes> <max-kb>
  if [ "$2" -gt "$(($3 * 1024))" ]; then
    printf 'mkrelease: over budget: %s (%s > %s)\n' "$1" "$2" "$(($3 * 1024))" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  return 0
}

write_receipt() {
  : > "$receipt"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do
    [ -n "$path" ] || continue
    set -- $(cksum "$stage/$path" 2>/dev/null)
    crc=$1
    bytes=$2
    check_budget "$path" "$bytes" "$maxkb"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$path" "$crc" "$bytes" >> "$receipt"
  done < "$build/MANIFEST"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mkrelease.sh — stage a release bundle out of a finished build tree.
#
# Build tree contract (produced by `make dist-tree`):
#   VERSION            single line: the release version
#   MANIFEST           one artifact per line: <path><TAB><max-kb>
#   <path>             the artifact files themselves (relative, no whitespace)
#
# Produces <outdir>/rel-<version>/ holding every artifact plus RECEIPT
# (one line per artifact: <path><TAB><cksum-crc><TAB><bytes>).
set -eu
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

log() { printf 'mkrelease: %s\n' "$1"; }

usage() {
  printf 'usage: mkrelease.sh <builddir> <outdir>\n' >&2
  exit 64
}

[ "$#" -eq 2 ] || usage
build=$1
out=$2
[ -d "$build" ] || { printf 'mkrelease: not a directory: %s\n' "$build" >&2; exit 66; }

version=''
stage=''
receipt=''

read_version() {
  local v=$(cat "$build/VERSION" 2>/dev/null)
  version=$v
  log "version $version"
}

stage_artifacts() {
  mkdir -p "$stage"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do
    [ -n "$path" ] || continue
    mkdir -p "$stage/$(dirname "$path")"
    cp "$build/$path" "$stage/$path" 2>/dev/null
    log "staged $path"
  done < "$build/MANIFEST"
  log "stage populated"
}

check_budget() { # <path> <bytes> <max-kb>
  if [ "$2" -gt "$(($3 * 1024))" ]; then
    printf 'mkrelease: over budget: %s (%s > %s)\n' "$1" "$2" "$(($3 * 1024))" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  return 0
}

write_receipt() {
  : > "$receipt"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do
    [ -n "$path" ] || continue
    set -- $(cksum "$stage/$path" 2>/dev/null)
    crc=$1
    bytes=$2
    check_budget "$path" "$bytes" "$maxkb"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$path" "$crc" "$bytes" >> "$receipt"
  done < "$build/MANIFEST"
  log "receipt written"
}

read_version
stage="$out/rel-$version"
receipt="$stage/RECEIPT"

if stage_artifacts; then
  log "artifacts in place"
else
  printf 'mkrelease: staging failed\n' >&2
  exit 70
fi

write_receipt && log "sealed"

log "release OK: rel-$version"

TASK
Release engineering ticket, severity raised after Thursday. mkrelease.sh stages release bundles out of finished build trees (VERSION file, MANIFEST of `<path><TAB><max-kb>` lines, artifact paths never contain whitespace) into `<outdir>/rel-<version>/` with a RECEIPT. It runs under `set -e`, which the whole team has been treating as a guarantee that a half-done release cannot happen. This month it happened three different ways:

1. A tree rsync'd from CI was missing assets/logo.png. The log cheerfully says `mkrelease: staged assets/logo.png` — for a file that does not exist — then the run face-plants with bash unbound-variable noise somewhere in the receipt step and exits 1. Nothing on stderr names the actual problem, and a half-populated rel-7.3.1/ was left sitting in the outdir for the deploy job to find.

2. media/big.bin came out of the build at 2048 bytes against its 1-KB manifest cap. The `mkrelease: over budget` warning is right there in stderr — immediately followed by `sealed` and `release OK`, exit 0. The pipeline shipped it.

3. Someone pointed the tool at a half-synced tree with no VERSION. It logged `mkrelease: version ` (blank), created a directory literally named `rel-`, and reported release OK. A tree with no MANIFEST at all is even better: instant success, empty receipt.

I want failures to actually fail: the right message on stderr, the right nonzero exit, and no rel-* directory left behind in the outdir on ANY failure — partial bundles are exactly how we got burned. The happy path must not change: its stdout log lines are grepped by the release dashboards and must stay byte-for-byte identical. Exit codes and messages for each failure are pinned in test_mkrelease.sh — that file is the contract, do not modify it; fix mkrelease.sh itself. Boxes involved include the macOS build minis, so keep whatever you touch portable.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mkrelease.sh — stage a release bundle out of a finished build tree.
#
# Build tree contract (produced by `make dist-tree`):
#   VERSION            single line: the release version
#   MANIFEST           one artifact per line: <path><TAB><max-kb>
#   <path>             the artifact files themselves (relative, no whitespace)
#
# Produces <outdir>/rel-<version>/ holding every artifact plus RECEIPT
# (one line per artifact: <path><TAB><cksum-crc><TAB><bytes>).
set -eu
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

log() { printf 'mkrelease: %s\n' "$1"; }

usage() {
  printf 'usage: mkrelease.sh <builddir> <outdir>\n' >&2
  exit 64
}

[ "$#" -eq 2 ] || usage
build=$1
out=$2
[ -d "$build" ] || { printf 'mkrelease: not a directory: %s\n' "$build" >&2; exit 66; }

version=''
stage=''
receipt=''

read_version() {
  local v=$(cat "$build/VERSION" 2>/dev/null)
  version=$v
  log "version $version"
}

stage_artifacts() {
  mkdir -p "$stage"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do

  done < "$build/MANIFEST"
  log "stage populated"
}

check_budget() { # <path> <bytes> <max-kb>
  if [ "$2" -gt "$(($3 * 1024))" ]; then

  return 0

Release engineering ticket, severity raised after Thursday. mkrelease.sh stages release bundles out of finished build trees (VERSION file, MANIFEST of `<path><TAB><max-kb>` lines, artifact paths never contain whitespace) into `<outdir>/rel-<version>/` with a RECEIPT. It runs under `set -e`, which the whole team has been treating as a guarantee that a half-done release cannot happen. This month it happened three different ways:

1. A tree rsync'd from CI was missing assets/logo.png. The log cheerfully says `mkrelease: staged assets/logo.png` — for a file that does not exist — then the run face-plants with bash unbound-variable noise somewhere in the receipt step and exits 1. 2. media/big.bin came out of the build at 2048 bytes against its 1-KB manifest cap. The `mkrelease: over budget` warning is right there in stderr — immediately followed by `sealed` and `release OK`, exit 0. The pipeline shipped it.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mkrelease.sh — stage a release bundle out of a finished build tree.
#
# Build tree contract (produced by `make dist-tree`):
#   VERSION            single line: the release version
#   MANIFEST           one artifact per line: <path><TAB><max-kb>
#   <path>             the artifact files themselves (relative, no whitespace)
#
# Produces <outdir>/rel-<version>/ holding every artifact plus RECEIPT
# (one line per artifact: <path><TAB><cksum-crc><TAB><bytes>).
set -eu
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

log() { printf 'mkrelease: %s\n' "$1"; }

usage() {
  printf 'usage: mkrelease.sh <builddir> <outdir>\n' >&2
  exit 64
}

[ "$#" -eq 2 ] || usage
build=$1
out=$2
[ -d "$build" ] || { printf 'mkrelease: not a directory: %s\n' "$build" >&2; exit 66; }

version=''
stage=''
receipt=''

read_version() {
  local v=$(cat "$build/VERSION" 2>/dev/null)
  version=$v
  log "version $version"
}

stage_artifacts() {
  mkdir -p "$stage"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do
    [ -n "$path" ] || continue
    mkdir -p "$stage/$(dirname "$path")"
    cp "$build/$path" "$stage/$path" 2>/dev/null
    log "staged $path"
  done < "$build/MANIFEST"
  log "stage populated"
}

check_budget() { # <path> <bytes> <max-kb>
  if [ "$2" -gt "$(($3 * 1024))" ]; then
    printf 'mkrelease: over budget: %s (%s > %s)\n' "$1" "$2" "$(($3 * 1024))" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  return 0
}

write_receipt() {
  : > "$receipt"
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r path maxkb; do
    [ -n "$path" ] || continue
    set -- $(cksum "$stage/$path" 2>/dev/null)
    crc=$1
    bytes=$2
    check_budget "$path" "$bytes" "$maxkb"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$path" "$crc" "$bytes" >> "$receipt"
  done < "$build/MANIFEST"
  log "receipt written"
}

read_version
stage="$out/rel-$version"
receipt="$stage/RECEIPT"

if stage_artifacts; then
  log "artifacts in place"
else
  printf 'mkrelease: staging failed\n' >&2
  exit 70
fi

write_receipt && log "sealed"

log "release OK: rel-$version"

Release engineering ticket, severity raised after Thursday. mkrelease.sh stages release bundles out of finished build trees (VERSION file, MANIFEST of `<path><TAB><max-kb>` lines, artifact paths never contain whitespace) into `<outdir>/rel-<version>/` with a RECEIPT. 1. A tree rsync'd from CI was missing assets/logo.png. The log cheerfully says `mkrelease: staged assets/logo.png` — for a file that does not exist — then the run face-plants with bash unbound-variable noise somewhere in the receipt step and exits 1. TASK
Release engineering ticket, severity raised after Thursday. mkrelease.sh stages release bundles out of finished build trees (VERSION file, MANIFEST of `<path><TAB><max-kb>` lines, artifact paths never contain whitespace) into `<outdir>/rel-<version>/` with a RECEIPT. It runs under `set -e`, which the whole team has been treating as a guarantee that a half-done release cannot happen. This month it happened three different ways:

1. A tree rsync'd from CI was missing assets/logo.png. The log cheerfully says `mkrelease: staged assets/logo.png` — for a file that does not exist — then the run face-plants with bash unbound-variable noise somewhere in the receipt step and exits 1. Nothing on stderr names the actual problem, and a half-populated rel-7.3.1/ was left sitting in the outdir for the deploy job to find.

2. media/big.bin came out of the build at 2048 bytes against its 1-KB manifest cap. The `mkrelease: over budget` warning is right there in stderr — immediately followed by `sealed` and `release OK`, exit 0. The pipeline shipped it.

3. Someone pointed the tool at a half-synced tree with no VERSION. It logged `mkrelease: version ` (blank), created a directory literally named `rel-`, and reported release OK. A tree with no MANIFEST at all is even better: instant success, empty receipt.

I want failures to actually fail: the right message on stderr, the right nonzero exit, and no rel-* directory left behind in the outdir on ANY failure — partial bundles are exactly how we got burned. The happy path must not change: its stdout log lines are grepped by the release dashboards and must stay byte-for-byte identical. Exit codes and messages for each failure are pinned in test_mkrelease.sh — that file is the contract, do not modify it; fix mkrelease.sh itself.
