TASK
Release engineering ticket, severity raised after Thursday. mkrelease.sh stages release bundles out of finished build trees (VERSION file, MANIFEST of `<path><TAB><max-kb>` lines, artifact paths never contain whitespace) into `<outdir>/rel-<version>/` with a RECEIPT. It runs under `set -e`, which the whole team has been treating as a guarantee that a half-done release cannot happen. This month it happened three different ways:

1. A tree rsync'd from CI was missing assets/logo.png. The log cheerfully says `mkrelease: staged assets/logo.png` — for a file that does not exist — then the run face-plants with bash unbound-variable noise somewhere in the receipt step and exits 1. Nothing on stderr names the actual problem, and a half-populated rel-7.3.1/ was left sitting in the outdir for the deploy job to find.

2. media/big.bin came out of the build at 2048 bytes against its 1-KB manifest cap. The `mkrelease: over budget` warning is right there in stderr — immediately followed by `sealed` and `release OK`, exit 0. The pipeline shipped it.

3. Someone pointed the tool at a half-synced tree with no VERSION. It logged `mkrelease: version ` (blank), created a directory literally named `rel-`, and reported release OK. A tree with no MANIFEST at all is even better: instant success, empty receipt.

I want failures to actually fail: the right message on stderr, the right nonzero exit, and no rel-* directory left behind in the outdir on ANY failure — partial bundles are exactly how we got burned. The happy path must not change: its stdout log lines are grepped by the release dashboards and must stay byte-for-byte identical. Exit codes and messages for each failure are pinned in test_mkrelease.sh — that file is the contract, do not modify it; fix mkrelease.sh itself. Boxes involved include the macOS build minis, so keep whatever you touch portable.

TASK
Our monorepo build tool describes internal components with little manifest files and we've started shipping import cycles that only blow up at link time. I want a proper analyzer library: module go-modcycles, package modcycles, stdlib only. Please structure it like a real project — manifest parsing, the graph, cycle enumeration, and topological ordering belong in separate files, not one giant modcycles.go.

The manifest format: every file ending in .mod, anywhere under a root directory (other files ignored). Lines are trimmed; blank lines and lines starting with # are comments. The first real line must be `module <name>`, exactly once per file; every following line is `import <name>`. Tokens are whitespace-separated (extra spaces fine). Names match [A-Za-z0-9_-]+ only. Parse errors, a missing/duplicate module line, junk directives, and importing the same name twice in one file are all Load errors that NAME THE FILE in the message; the same module declared in two files is an error naming the module. Modules may import modules nobody declares — that is NOT a load error, people delete manifests all the time.

API: Load(root string) (*Graph, error), then on the graph: Modules() []string sorted; Imports(name) ([]string, bool) in declaration order; Missing() []string — sorted, deduplicated names that are imported but declared nowhere.

Cycles() [][]string is the heart of it: EVERY elementary cycle in the import graph, self-imports included as a one-element cycle. Each cycle is written as the full path — consecutive elements follow import edges and the last element imports the first — rotated to start at its alphabetically smallest member, and the outer list sorted lexicographically element-by-element. Same tree in, byte-identical report out, every single run; the tool diffs these reports in CI.

Order() ([]string, error): dependency-first topological order over declared modules (imports of undeclared names just don't count), and when several modules are simultaneously ready, alphabetical order picks next — again, fully deterministic. If the graph has any cycle, Order returns an error whose text contains "cycle".

Acceptance is load_test.go + cycles_test.go, run with go test -race -timeout 30s ./... — those files are frozen. Keep it stdlib.

`runbook-verify` is the Bash 5 harness for checking copy-pasteable runbook commands without touching live state. Run it from the repository root as `bash runbook-verify --fixtures DIR --report FILE RUNBOOK...`. A verification block is a Markdown fence whose opening line is exactly ` ```verify id=ID safety=SAFETY fixture=FIXTURE expected=EXPECTED` (without the leading space shown here). Values contain no whitespace. FIXTURE is a directory below DIR and EXPECTED is a file below that fixture; both must be relative paths without empty, `.` or `..` components. Other Markdown and other kinds of code fences are prose only. Malformed or unterminated `verify` fences are failures.

Only blocks whose safety value is exactly `safe` may execute. Every other safety value is reported as `SKIP`, and neither its body nor its fixture metadata may be evaluated. A safe block runs with Bash in a private copy of its local fixture. It passes only when it exits zero, writes no stderr, and its stdout is byte-for-byte equal to the declared expected file in the original fixture. Private copies must be removed on success and failure. The output report is deterministic: it contains no timestamps or scratch paths, preserves runbook argument and block order, records the Bash and `cmp` versions, gives one result per verification block, and ends with pass/fail/skip counters. Any failure makes the harness exit 1. Invocation errors exit 64. Exact report spelling and precedence are pinned by `tests/test_runbook_verify.sh`.

The harness is almost complete, but its successful-output comparison loses trailing newline bytes before comparing. Consequently output that differs from the expected file only by final newlines can be accepted. Fix this focused defect without changing the runbook format, safety boundary, fixture isolation, report contract, or protected test. Do not modify `tests/test_runbook_verify.sh`.

#!/usr/bin/env zsh
# printsum.zsh — nightly print-accounting summary over the print-server feed.
#
# Feed: one job per line,  printer|user|pages  (pipe-separated, three fields).
# Lines starting with # and blank lines are exporter padding: skipped quietly.
# Any other field count is malformed: warn on stderr, skip, keep going.
#
# WATCH: printers billed back to their owning departments. Space-separated,
# reported in exactly this order.
WATCH="annex lobby-a"

usage() {
  echo "usage: printsum.zsh <feed-file>" >&2
  exit 64
}

[ "$#" -eq 1 ] || usage
feed=$1
if [ ! -f "$feed" ] || [ ! -r "$feed" ]; then
  echo "printsum.zsh: cannot read: $feed" >&2
  exit 66
fi

declare -A jobs_by pages_by users_seen
declare -a seen
declare -i lineno=0 jobs_total=0 pages_total=0

while IFS= read -r line; do
  lineno=$(( lineno + 1 ))
  [ -z "$line" ] && continue
  case $line in '#'*) continue ;; esac
  f=($(printf '%s\n' "$line" | tr '|' ' '))
  if [ "${#f[@]}" -ne 3 ]; then
    echo "printsum.zsh: line $lineno: malformed, skipped" >&2
    continue
  fi
  printer=${f[0]}
  user=${f[1]}
  pages=${f[2]}
  if [ -z "${jobs_by[$printer]:-}" ]; then
    seen+=("$printer")
  fi
  jobs_by[$printer]=$(( ${jobs_by[$printer]:-0} + 1 ))
  pages_by[$printer]=$(( ${pages_by[$printer]:-0} + pages ))
  users_seen[$user]=1
  jobs_total=$(( jobs_total + 1 ))
  pages_total=$(( pages_total + pages ))
done < "$feed"

echo "USAGE"
if [ "${#seen[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
  printf '%s\n' "${seen[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort | while IFS= read -r p; do
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$p" "${jobs_by[$p]}" "${pages_by[$p]}"
  done
fi
echo "WATCHED"
for w in $WATCH; do
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$w" "${pages_by[$w]:-0}"
done
echo "TOTALS"
printf 'jobs\t%s\n' "$jobs_total"
printf 'printers\t%s\n' "${#seen[@]}"
printf 'users\t%s\n' "${#users_seen[@]}"
printf 'pages\t%s\n' "$pages_total"

#!/usr/bin/env zsh
# Acceptance harness for printsum.zsh.
# Run from the workspace root:  zsh test_printsum.zsh
emulate -R zsh
setopt no_unset
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL
unset CDPATH cdpath 2>/dev/null

# run from the harness's own directory even if invoked from elsewhere
[[ $0 == */* ]] && cd -- ${0:h}

zmodload zsh/mapfile

ROOT=$PWD
T=_t
rm -rf "$T"
mkdir -p "$T"
trap 'rm -rf "$ROOT/$T"' EXIT

typeset -i checks=0 fails=0

assert_eq() { # assert_eq <label> <expected> <actual>
  (( checks += 1 ))
  if [[ "$2" == "$3" ]]; then
    return 0
  fi
  (( fails += 1 ))
  printf 'FAIL %s\n--- expected ---\n%s\n--- actual ---\n%s\n----------------\n' "$1" "$2" "$3"
}

mkexp() { # mkexp <var> <line>... -- join lines with \n plus trailing newline
  local __n=$1
  shift
  : ${(P)__n::=${(F)@}$'\n'}
}

RC=0
OUT=''
ERR=''
run() { # run <cmd...> -- capture RC, OUT, ERR byte-exactly
  "$@" > "$ROOT/$T/out" 2> "$ROOT/$T/err"
  RC=$?
  OUT=${mapfile[$ROOT/$T/out]-}
  ERR=${mapfile[$ROOT/$T/err]-}
}

expect() { # expect <label> <rc> <expected-stdout> <expected-stderr>
  assert_eq "$1: exit code" "$2" "$RC"
  assert_eq "$1: stdout" "$3" "$OUT"
  assert_eq "$1: stderr" "$4" "$ERR"
}

if [[ ! -f printsum.zsh ]]; then
  print -r -- 'FAIL printsum.zsh not found in the workspace root'
  exit 1
fi
if [[ ! -f queue_feed.txt ]]; then
  print -r -- 'FAIL queue_feed.txt not found in the workspace root'
  exit 1

#!/usr/bin/env zsh

#
# Feed: one job per line,  printer|user|pages  (pipe-separated, three fields).

usage() {

  exit 64

[ "$#" -eq 1 ] || usage

  echo "printsum.zsh: cannot read: $feed" >&2
  exit 66
fi

declare -A jobs_by pages_by users_seen
declare -a seen
declare -i lineno=0 jobs_total=0 pages_total=0

while IFS= read -r line; do
  lineno=$(( lineno + 1 ))

  pages_by[$printer]=$(( ${pages_by[$printer]:-0} + pages ))
  users_seen[$user]=1
  jobs_total=$(( jobs_total + 1 ))
  pages_total=$(( pages_total + pages ))

TASK
We got burned: a job name with a space in it went through cmdline.String() into a remote sh -c and executed half a filename as a command. Security review filed three requirements against the cmdline package before the job runner is allowed to ship command lines anywhere. The existing builder API (New/Append/Args/String) stays exactly as-is — String is all over the audit logs and its naive join is intentional there.

1. Command.Quoted() string — a POSIX-shell-safe rendering. An element passes through bare only when it is non-empty and every character is alphanumeric or one of _ @ % + = : , . / - (dash). Anything else gets wrapped in single quotes with embedded single quotes escaped the standard way ('\''); the empty string renders as ''. The executable name gets the same treatment as the args.

2. Command.Expand(vars map[string]string, mode ExpandMode) (*Command, error) — substitute ${NAME} references (NAME = letters, digits, underscore, not starting with a digit) everywhere in the command, from the map only, never from the process environment. Two modes: Strict errors on a reference with no entry in the map and the error must name the variable; Lenient substitutes the empty string. A ${ with no closing brace is an error in BOTH modes. A bare $ without braces is not a reference and passes through untouched. Returns a new Command; the receiver must not be modified.

3. Command.Fill(bindings map[string]string) (*Command, error) — our job templates say things like convert {input} --out={output}. A placeholder is {name} where name is lowercase letters/digits/underscore starting with a letter; anything else in braces (awk scripts, {FOO}, unclosed braces) is literal. Validation is two-way: a placeholder without a binding is an error naming it, and a binding that never gets used is ALSO an error naming it — that second one would have caught the outptu typo that shipped a broken template last month. Same immutability rule as Expand.

shellsafe_test.go is the acceptance suite; cmdline_test.go pins the current builder and keeps passing. Don't edit either test file. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... decides.

TASK
Partner API started enforcing quotas for real this week:

  429 Too Many Requests — quota: 30 requests per rolling 10s — retry-after: 4

'Rolling' is the operative word — our fixed-bucket limiter bursts 60 across a bucket boundary and they still 429 us. Build ratelimit.ts exporting class SlidingWindowLimiter.

Constructor takes { limit, windowMs, timers? }. Semantics: an acquisition holds a slot for windowMs from the moment it was GRANTED (not requested), and at most `limit` grants may exist inside any rolling window. acquire(signal?) resolves immediately while slots are free, otherwise queues; queued callers get slots strictly FIFO as old grants age out (a grant from t is free again at exactly t+windowMs; several can free at once). AbortSignal support because our HTTP layer times out: pre-aborted signal rejects with its reason without queueing; aborting while queued rejects the waiter, drops it from the queue, and must NOT burn a slot or disturb the order of everyone behind it. Also tryAcquire(): boolean — grab a free slot synchronously or return false, never queue, never jump ahead of queued waiters. Expose `pending` (number of queued waiters). Throw TypeError from the constructor for a non-positive-integer limit or windowMs <= 0.

timers is { now, setTimeout, clearTimeout } defaulting to the real ones; the acceptance tests (test_ratelimit.ts, `node --test test_ratelimit.ts`) drive a fake clock through it, so all waiting must go through timers — no Date.now() or bare setTimeout anywhere. Tests are the contract; don't edit them. No dependencies.

TASK
The theming engine needs one color module instead of the three half-broken helpers we copy-paste around. Please write color.ts with these exports — test_color.ts is the acceptance contract (`node --test test_color.ts`, don't edit it):

parseHex(input) -> { r, g, b, a }. r/g/b are 0-255 integers, a is 0..1. Accept 3-, 6- and 8-digit forms, hash optional, case-insensitive; 3-digit expands per CSS (#abc == #aabbcc); 8-digit carries alpha in the last byte. Anything else — wrong length, bad chars — throws TypeError.

toHex(color) -> lowercase '#rrggbb', or '#rrggbbaa' only when alpha < 1 (missing alpha means opaque). Out-of-range channels get CLAMPED to 0-255 (alpha to 0..1) and fractional channels rounded — designers feed us r: 300 and r: -20 all day, it must not throw.

rgbToHsl({ r, g, b }) -> { h, s, l } with h in [0, 360) degrees, s and l as 0-100 percentages. Achromatic colors report h: 0, s: 0. Don't round these — the tests allow small float tolerance.

hslToRgb({ h, s, l }) -> integer { r, g, b }. Hue wraps modulo 360 (negative too: -30 == 330), s and l clamp to 0-100.

mix(c1, c2, t) -> linear interpolation of r, g, b and a at t, with t clamped to [0,1] and channels rounded to integers. Colors without a mix as opaque.

Stdlib only, no npm.

I am done debugging stringly-typed config. Our edge service reads an INI-ish file and today it's all raw HashMap<String,String> lookups with unwraps sprinkled around — last outage was literally `port = fast` taking a worker fleet down at 3am with a panic and no location info. I want a proper two-layer loader in this crate (rs-cfgparse), src/lib.rs, no serde, no crates — hand-rolled typed extraction with REAL error values: every single error carries a 1-based (line, col), character-counted. Acceptance tests are in tests/config.rs; tests/, Cargo.toml, and .gitignore are off limits.

Layer 1 — RawConfig::parse(src: &str) -> Result<RawConfig, ParseError>. Format: lines are blank (skip), comments ('#' as the first non-blank character — a '#' inside a value is DATA), section headers `[name]` (optional indentation; '[' position is the section's position; missing ']' = UnclosedSection at the '[' col; non-space text after ']' = TrailingChars at that char's col), or `key = value` (split on the FIRST '='; key and value trimmed of spaces/tabs). No '=' on a non-header line, or an empty key = BadLine at the line's first non-blank col. Empty value = MissingValue at the '=' col. A key before any section header = KeyOutsideSection at the key's col. The same key twice in one section = DuplicateKey(key) at the SECOND occurrence's key col; reopening a section later is legal and accumulates keys (duplicates still collide across reopenings). Tabs count as one column. Tolerate CRLF (strip a trailing \r per line). RawConfig exposes get(&self, section, key) -> Option<&RawValue> where pub struct RawValue { pub text: String, pub line: usize, pub col: usize } (col = first char of the trimmed value), and section_pos(&self, name) -> Option<(usize, usize)> (the '[' position).

Layer 2 — pub fn load_server_config(src: &str) -> Result<ServerConfig, ConfigError> extracting section [server] into pub struct ServerConfig { pub host: String, pub port: u16, pub tls: bool, pub workers: u32, pub log_level: LogLevel, pub allow: Vec<String> } with pub enum LogLevel { Error, Warn, Info, Debug }. Field order host, port, tls, workers, log_level, allow; host and port required, the rest default to false / 4 / Info / empty vec. Rules: integers are optional-'-' then digits (anything else: WrongType expected "integer"), port must land in 1..=65535 and workers in 1..=512 or it's BadValue with message "port must be between 1 and 65535" / "workers must be between 1 and 512" (a digits-only value too big for i64 also gets the range message, never a panic); tls is exactly "true"/"false" (WrongType expected "boolean" otherwise — "True" doesn't fly); log_level is exactly one of error/warn/info/debug else BadValue "unknown log level \"<got>\""; allow splits on ',' with per-item trim, any empty item = BadValue "empty entry in allow list". Unknown keys are ignored. Positions: WrongType/BadValue point at the VALUE; a Missing key points at its section's '[' header; a missing [server] section reports the FIRST field in extraction order (host) at (1,1).

Error architecture — this is the part I care about, get it exactly right: pub struct ParseError { pub line, pub col, pub kind: ParseKind } with pub enum ParseKind { BadLine, UnclosedSection, TrailingChars, MissingValue, DuplicateKey(String), KeyOutsideSection }; pub struct FieldError { pub line, pub col, pub section: String, pub key: String, pub kind: FieldKind } with pub enum FieldKind { Missing, WrongType { expected: &'static str, got: String }, BadValue(String) }; pub enum ConfigError { Parse(ParseError), Field(FieldError) } with impl From<ParseError> and impl From<FieldError> (extraction code should be using `?` through those), accessor methods line()/col() on ConfigError, Display + std::error::Error on ConfigError rendering "line L, col C: ..." tap(fn) builds a pass-through step: it runs fn(value) for the side effect and yields value onward. If fn returns a promise, wait for it first (still yielding the original value); if fn throws or rejects, that failure propagates like any other step failure.

TASK
Ticket: in-memory job orchestrator for the media-processing worker.

Today every worker binary hand-rolls its own goroutine soup for "run these jobs, respect their dependencies, don't melt the box", and we've been bitten by all of them. I want one library, package jobflow (module go-jobflow, repo root), that owns this. Split it into a few focused files — types/validation, graph checks, the scheduler, status bookkeeping — whatever cut you like, just not one monolith.

API the tests compile against: JobID and State string types with constants StatePending/StateRunning/StateSucceeded/StateFailed/StateSkipped/StateCancelled (values "pending", "running", "succeeded", "failed", "skipped", "cancelled"); JobSpec{ID JobID; Deps []JobID; Priority int; Run func(context.Context) error}; Options{MaxParallel int}; New(Options) (*Orchestrator, error); (*Orchestrator).Add(JobSpec) error; (*Orchestrator).Run(ctx) (map[JobID]State, error); (*Orchestrator).Status(JobID) (State, error).

Rules of the road: New rejects MaxParallel < 1. Add rejects empty IDs, nil Run funcs and duplicates (name the job in the error) and is refused once Run has been called; deps may point at jobs added later. Run is single-use, validates the whole graph up front (unknown dep errors name the dep, cycle errors contain the word "cycle") and then executes EVERY added job: a job starts only after all its deps succeeded, at most MaxParallel jobs run at once, and when a slot frees the highest-Priority ready job takes it (ties by Add order; jobs released by the same completion are weighed together). If a job errors it's failed, its transitive dependents are skipped and never invoked, unrelated branches keep going, and Run's error wraps the job's error (errors.Is-visible) and names it. Cancellation is the part I care most about, because it's where the old code always raced: every job gets a context derived from Run's; the moment that context is cancelled NO further job may be picked up — check the context at every dispatch decision, don't rely on a select branch winning — in-flight jobs are waited for (whatever they return decides succeeded/failed), and every job that never started ends up cancelled, taking precedence over would-be skip marking; Run then returns the final map plus an error satisfying errors.Is(err, context.Canceled). The returned map always covers every added job, even on failure or cancel. Status answers at any moment — before Run (pending), while things execute (running), after (terminal states) — so it must be safe under concurrent use; unknown IDs are an error.

jobflow_test.go is the acceptance contract — read it before designing, don't edit it. Green means `go test -race -timeout 30s ./...` and it has to pass every time, not most times: the suite gates everything on channels and will call out both serialized execution and over-parallel execution.

Ticket: in-memory job orchestrator for the media-processing worker.

Today every worker binary hand-rolls its own goroutine soup for "run these jobs, respect their dependencies, don't melt the box", and we've been bitten by all of them. I want one library, package jobflow (module go-jobflow, repo root), that owns this. Split it into a few focused files — types/validation, graph checks, the scheduler, status bookkeeping — whatever cut you like, just not one monolith.

API the tests compile against: JobID and State string types with constants StatePending/StateRunning/StateSucceeded/StateFailed/StateSkipped/StateCancelled (values "pending", "running", "succeeded", "failed", "skipped", "cancelled"); JobSpec{ID JobID; Deps []JobID; Priority int; Run func(context.Context) error}; Options{MaxParallel int}; New(Options) (*Orchestrator, error); (*Orchestrator).Add(JobSpec) error; (*Orchestrator).Run(ctx) (map[JobID]State, error); (*Orchestrator).Status(JobID) (State, error).

Rules of the road: New rejects MaxParallel < 1. Add rejects empty IDs, nil Run funcs and duplicates (name the job in the error) and is refused once Run has been called; deps may point at jobs added later. Run is single-use, validates the whole graph up front (unknown dep errors name the dep, cycle errors contain the word "cycle") and then executes EVERY added job: a job starts only after all its deps succeeded, at most MaxParallel jobs run at once, and when a slot frees the highest-Priority ready job takes it (ties by Add order; jobs released by the same completion are weighed together). If a job errors it's failed, its transitive dependents are skipped and never invoked, unrelated branches keep going, and Run's error wraps the job's error (errors.Is-visible) and names it. Cancellation is the part I care most about, because it's where the old code always raced: every job gets a context derived from Run's; the moment that context is cancelled NO further job may be picked up — check the context at every dispatch decision, don't rely on a select branch winning — in-flight jobs are waited for (whatever they return decides succeeded/failed), and every job that never started ends up cancelled, taking precedence over would-be skip marking; Run then returns the final map plus an error satisfying errors.Is(err, context.Canceled). The returned map always covers every added job, even on failure or cancel. Status answers at any moment — before Run (pending), while things execute (running), after (terminal states) — so it must be safe under concurrent use; unknown IDs are an error.

Ticket: in-memory job orchestrator for the media-processing worker.

Today every worker binary hand-rolls its own goroutine soup for "run these jobs, respect their dependencies, don't melt the box", and we've been bitten by all of them. I want one library, package jobflow (module go-jobflow, repo root), that owns this. Split it into a few focused files — types/validation, graph checks, the scheduler, status bookkeeping — whatever cut you like, just not one monolith.

API the tests compile against: JobID and State string types with constants StatePending/StateRunning/StateSucceeded/StateFailed/StateSkipped/StateCancelled (values "pending", "running", "succeeded", "failed", "skipped", "cancelled"); JobSpec{ID JobID; Deps []JobID; Priority int; Run func(context.Context) error}; Options{MaxParallel int}; New(Options) (*Orchestrator, error); (*Orchestrator).Add(JobSpec) error; (*Orchestrator).Run(ctx) (map[JobID]State, error); (*Orchestrator).Status(JobID) (State, error).

Rules of the road: New rejects MaxParallel < 1. Add rejects empty IDs, nil Run funcs and duplicates (name the job in the error) and is refused once Run has been called; deps may point at jobs added later. Run is single-use, validates the whole graph up front (unknown dep errors name the dep, cycle errors contain the word "cycle") and then executes EVERY added job: a job starts only after all its deps succeeded, at most MaxParallel jobs run at once, and when a slot frees the highest-Priority ready job takes it (ties by Add order; jobs released by the same completion are weighed together). If a job errors it's failed, its transitive dependents are skipped and never invoked, unrelated branches keep going, and Run's error wraps the job's error (errors.Is-visible) and names it. Cancellation is the part I care most about, because it's where the old code always raced: every job gets a context derived from Run's; the moment that context is cancelled NO further job may be picked up — check the context at every dispatch decision, don't rely on a select branch winning — in-flight jobs are waited for (whatever they return decides succeeded/failed), and every job that never started ends up cancelled, taking precedence over would-be skip marking; Run then returns the final map plus an error satisfying errors.Is(err, context.Canceled). The returned map always covers every added job, even on failure or cancel. Status answers at any moment — before Run (pending), while things execute (running), after (terminal states) — so it must be safe under concurrent use; unknown IDs are an error.

TASK
Ticket: in-memory job orchestrator for the media-processing worker.

Today every worker binary hand-rolls its own goroutine soup for "run these jobs, respect their dependencies, don't melt the box", and we've been bitten by all of them. I want one library, package jobflow (module go-jobflow, repo root), that owns this. Split it into a few focused files — types/validation, graph checks, the scheduler, status bookkeeping — whatever cut you like, just not one monolith.

API the tests compile against: JobID and State string types with constants StatePending/StateRunning/StateSucceeded/StateFailed/StateSkipped/StateCancelled (values "pending", "running", "succeeded", "failed", "skipped", "cancelled"); JobSpec{ID JobID; Deps []JobID; Priority int; Run func(context.Context) error}; Options{MaxParallel int}; New(Options) (*Orchestrator, error); (*Orchestrator).Add(JobSpec) error; (*Orchestrator).Run(ctx) (map[JobID]State, error); (*Orchestrator).Status(JobID) (State, error).

Rules of the road: New rejects MaxParallel < 1. Add rejects empty IDs, nil Run funcs and duplicates (name the job in the error) and is refused once Run has been called; deps may point at jobs added later. Run is single-use, validates the whole graph up front (unknown dep errors name the dep, cycle errors contain the word "cycle") and then executes EVERY added job: a job starts only after all its deps succeeded, at most MaxParallel jobs run at once, and when a slot frees the highest-Priority ready job takes it (ties by Add order; jobs released by the same completion are weighed together). If a job errors it's failed, its transitive dependents are skipped and never invoked, unrelated branches keep going, and Run's error wraps the job's error (errors.Is-visible) and names it. Cancellation is the part I care most about, because it's where the old code always raced: every job gets a context derived from Run's; the moment that context is cancelled NO further job may be picked up — check the context at every dispatch decision, don't rely on a select branch winning — in-flight jobs are waited for (whatever they return decides succeeded/failed), and every job that never started ends up cancelled, taking precedence over would-be skip marking; Run then returns the final map plus an error satisfying errors.Is(err, context.Canceled). The returned map always covers every added job, even on failure or cancel. Status answers at any moment — before Run (pending), while things execute (running), after (terminal states) — so it must be safe under concurrent use; unknown IDs are an error.

jobflow_test.go is the acceptance contract — read it before designing, don't edit it. Green means `go test -race -timeout 30s ./...` and it has to pass every time, not most times: the suite gates everything on channels and will call out both serialized execution and over-parallel execution.

TASK
Ticket: in-memory job orchestrator for the media-processing worker.

Today every worker binary hand-rolls its own goroutine soup for "run these jobs, respect their dependencies, don't melt the box", and we've been bitten by all of them. I want one library, package jobflow (module go-jobflow, repo root), that owns this. Split it into a few focused files — types/validation, graph checks, the scheduler, status bookkeeping — whatever cut you like, just not one monolith.

API the tests compile against: JobID and State string types with constants StatePending/StateRunning/StateSucceeded/StateFailed/StateSkipped/StateCancelled (values "pending", "running", "succeeded", "failed", "skipped", "cancelled"); JobSpec{ID JobID; Deps []JobID; Priority int; Run func(context.Context) error}; Options{MaxParallel int}; New(Options) (*Orchestrator, error); (*Orchestrator).Add(JobSpec) error; (*Orchestrator).Run(ctx) (map[JobID]State, error); (*Orchestrator).Status(JobID) (State, error).

Rules of the road: New rejects MaxParallel < 1. Add rejects empty IDs, nil Run funcs and duplicates (name the job in the error) and is refused once Run has been called; deps may point at jobs added later. Run is single-use, validates the whole graph up front (unknown dep errors name the dep, cycle errors contain the word "cycle") and then executes EVERY added job: a job starts only after all its deps succeeded, at most MaxParallel jobs run at once, and when a slot frees the highest-Priority ready job takes it (ties by Add order; jobs released by the same completion are weighed together). If a job errors it's failed, its transitive dependents are skipped and never invoked, unrelated branches keep going, and Run's error wraps the job's error (errors.Is-visible) and names it. Cancellation is the part I care most about, because it's where the old code always raced: every job gets a context derived from Run's; the moment that context is cancelled NO further job may be picked up — check the context at every dispatch decision, don't rely on a select branch winning — in-flight jobs are waited for (whatever they return decides succeeded/failed), and every job that never started ends up cancelled, taking precedence over would-be skip marking; Run then returns the final map plus an error satisfying errors.Is(err, context.Canceled). The returned map always covers every added job, even on failure or cancel. Status answers at any moment — before Run (pending), while things execute (running), after (terminal states) — so it must be safe under concurrent use; unknown IDs are an error.

jobflow_test.go is the acceptance contract — read it before designing, don't edit it. Green means `go test -race -timeout 30s ./...` and it has to pass every time, not most times: the suite gates everything on channels and will call out both serialized execution and over-parallel execution.

TASK
Ticket: in-memory job orchestrator for the media-processing worker.

Today every worker binary hand-rolls its own goroutine soup for "run these jobs, respect their dependencies, don't melt the box", and we've been bitten by all of them. I want one library, package jobflow (module go-jobflow, repo root), that owns this. Split it into a few focused files — types/validation, graph checks, the scheduler, status bookkeeping — whatever cut you like, just not one monolith.

API the tests compile against: JobID and State string types with constants StatePending/StateRunning/StateSucceeded/StateFailed/StateSkipped/StateCancelled (values "pending", "running", "succeeded", "failed", "skipped", "cancelled"); JobSpec{ID JobID; Deps []JobID; Priority int; Run func(context.Context) error}; Options{MaxParallel int}; New(Options) (*Orchestrator, error); (*Orchestrator).Add(JobSpec) error; (*Orchestrator).Run(ctx) (map[JobID]State, error); (*Orchestrator).Status(JobID) (State, error).

Rules of the road: New rejects MaxParallel < 1. Add rejects empty IDs, nil Run funcs and duplicates (name the job in the error) and is refused once Run has been called; deps may point at jobs added later. Run is single-use, validates the whole graph up front (unknown dep errors name the dep, cycle errors contain the word "cycle") and then executes EVERY added job: a job starts only after all its deps succeeded, at most MaxParallel jobs run at once, and when a slot frees the highest-Priority ready job takes it (ties by Add order; jobs released by the same completion are weighed together). If a job errors it's failed, its transitive dependents are skipped and never invoked, unrelated branches keep going, and Run's error wraps the job's error (errors.Is-visible) and names it. Cancellation is the part I care most about, because it's where the old code always raced: every job gets a context derived from Run's; the moment that context is cancelled NO further job may be picked up — check the context at every dispatch decision, don't rely on a select branch winning — in-flight jobs are waited for (whatever they return decides succeeded/failed), and every job that never started ends up cancelled, taking precedence over would-be skip marking; Run then returns the final map plus an error satisfying errors.Is(err, context.Canceled). The returned map always covers every added job, even on failure or cancel. Status answers at any moment — before Run (pending), while things execute (running), after (terminal states) — so it must be safe under concurrent use; unknown IDs are an error.

jobflow_test.go is the acceptance contract — read it before designing, don't edit it. Green means `go test -race -timeout 30s ./...` and it has to pass every time, not most times: the suite gates everything on channels and will call out both serialized execution and over-parallel execution.

// Order totals: subtotal minus discount, plus tax, plus shipping.
//
// Contract with finance: whatever we charge is an exact integer count of
// cents — the ledger export rejects anything else. Tax applies to the
// discounted goods amount, never to shipping.
import type { Session } from './session.ts';
import { cartSubtotalCents, discountCents } from './discounts.ts';

export const TAX_RATE = 0.07;
export const SHIP_FLAT_CENTS = 599;
export const FREE_SHIP_MIN_CENTS = 5000;

export function shippingCents(netCents: number): number {
  return netCents >= FREE_SHIP_MIN_CENTS ? 0 : SHIP_FLAT_CENTS;
}

export function orderTotalCents(session: Session): number {
  const sub = cartSubtotalCents(session.items);
  const off = session.appliedCode
    ? discountCents(session.appliedCode, session.items)
    : 0;
  const net = sub - off;
  const shipping = shippingCents(net);

  if (off > 0) {
    // Discounted carts: the tax arithmetic reads more naturally in dollars.
    const netDollars = net / 100;
    const withTax = netDollars + netDollars * TAX_RATE;
    return withTax * 100 + shipping;
  }

  return net + Math.round(net * TAX_RATE) + shipping;
}

I've reproduced all three bugs. Let me map the 6 failures to root causes:

**Bug 1 (stale/cross-contaminated promo)** — `discountCents` memoizes on `code + ':' + items.length`. That key is identical when (a) a qty changes without changing line count → stale discount (ord-4 → ord-5 inherits 500), and (b) two different single-line carts use SAVE10 → cross-shopper bleed (ord-6a's 110 reused for ord-6b). The "$50 cart → $1.10 off" is exactly 110 cents bleeding from a prior $11 single-line cart.

**Bug 2 (non-integer cents)** — `orderTotalCents` switches to floating-point dollars (`netDollars + netDollars*TAX_RATE`) only when a promo applies, yielding `4159.960000000001`.

**Bug 3 (double refund)** — `requestRefund` checks `refundedTotal + amount <= paid`, then `await capture`, then pushes. Two overlapping calls both pass the check before either pushes.

Now the fixes.

Last month a box lost power and our homegrown settings cache came back empty — it buffered writes in memory and flushed 'eventually'. Never again. I want a small append-only KV store where every acknowledged write is already in the log file when the call returns.

Module go-kvlog, package kvlog, this repo. API: Open(path string) (*Store, error) — creates the WAL if missing, replays it if present; (*Store).Set(key, value string) error; Get(key string) (string, bool); Delete(key string) error; Len() int (count of live keys); Compact() error; Close() error. Set/Delete/Compact after Close must return errors. Keys and values are arbitrary strings — embedded newlines, tabs, NUL bytes, unicode, multi-KB values, and the empty string as a VALUE is real data: after Set(k, "") a Get(k) returns ("", true), which is not the same as a missing key. Delete of a missing key is a quiet no-op. The store must be safe for concurrent use from multiple goroutines.

Durability rules — and be aware the tests literally copy the live WAL file to a new path mid-run (no Close) to simulate the power cut, then Open the copy:
- when Set/Delete return, the operation is fully in the file. No user-space buffering you don't flush before acknowledging.
- torn tail: a crash can chop bytes off the end of the file. Open on such a log must succeed, recover every record before the tear, and NEVER surface a half-written value — the final operation is either completely there or completely gone. Design the record format so a truncated record is detectable (the tests cut 1-3 bytes off the end and check that the last key either has its exact full value or is absent).
- after recovering a torn log the store keeps working: new Sets append and the file replays cleanly on the next Open — don't leave the partial garbage sitting in the middle of the log.
- replay applies operations in order: last Set wins, Delete removes.
- Compact() rewrites the log down to just the live state, in a way that is itself crash-safe to read back: after ~10x overwrite churn plus deletes the file must shrink to under half its pre-compaction size, state identical, still identical after reopen, and appends after compaction must survive further reopens.

store_test.go and recovery_test.go are the contract; do not touch them. go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass. I'd split record encoding / replay / compaction / the store API into separate files — your call, but not one monolith.

Module go-kvlog, package kvlog, this repo. My design:
- **Record format**: `[4-byte LE payloadLen][4-byte LE CRC32(payload)][payload]`, where payload = `[1-byte op][4-byte LE keyLen][key][4-byte LE valLen][value]`. The CRC + explicit length makes any torn tail unambiguously detectable.
- **Durability**: each Set/Delete does `Write` + `Sync` (fsync) before returning, under the write lock.
- **Torn-tail recovery**: Open replays records, records the offset after the last *valid* record, then `Truncate`s the file to that offset so the partial garbage doesn't sit ahead of future appends.
- **Compaction**: write live state to a temp file, fsync, atomic rename, reopen fd.

- **Record format**: `[4-byte LE payloadLen][4-byte LE CRC32(payload)][payload]`, where payload = `[1-byte op][4-byte LE keyLen][key][4-byte LE valLen][value]`. The CRC + explicit length makes any torn tail unambiguously detectable.

Module go-kvlog, package kvlog, this repo. - replay applies operations in order: last Set wins, Delete removes.

Last month a box lost power and our homegrown settings cache came back empty — it buffered writes in memory and flushed 'eventually'. Never again. I want a small append-only KV store where every acknowledged write is already in the log file when the call returns.

Module go-kvlog, package kvlog, this repo. API: Open(path string) (*Store, error) — creates the WAL if missing, replays it if present; (*Store).Set(key, value string) error; Get(key string) (string, bool); Delete(key string) error; Len() int (count of live keys); Compact() error; Close() error. Set/Delete/Compact after Close must return errors. Keys and values are arbitrary strings — embedded newlines, tabs, NUL bytes, unicode, multi-KB values, and the empty string as a VALUE is real data: after Set(k, "") a Get(k) returns ("", true), which is not the same as a missing key. Delete of a missing key is a quiet no-op. The store must be safe for concurrent use from multiple goroutines.

Durability rules — and be aware the tests literally copy the live WAL file to a new path mid-run (no Close) to simulate the power cut, then Open the copy:
- when Set/Delete return, the operation is fully in the file. No user-space buffering you don't flush before acknowledging.
- torn tail: a crash can chop bytes off the end of the file. Open on such a log must succeed, recover every record before the tear, and NEVER surface a half-written value — the final operation is either completely there or completely gone. Design the record format so a truncated record is detectable (the tests cut 1-3 bytes off the end and check that the last key either has its exact full value or is absent).
- after recovering a torn log the store keeps working: new Sets append and the file replays cleanly on the next Open — don't leave the partial garbage sitting in the middle of the log.
- replay applies operations in order: last Set wins, Delete removes.
- Compact() rewrites the log down to just the live state, in a way that is itself crash-safe to read back: after ~10x overwrite churn plus deletes the file must shrink to under half its pre-compaction size, state identical, still identical after reopen, and appends after compaction must survive further reopens.

TASK
I run the scan station for the county archive digitization project. Every batch lands as a directory of files with whatever names the scanner and the volunteers' cameras invented — `IMG 0007.JPG`, `clip.mov`, bare `notes` — and before ingest they all have to follow our sequence scheme. I've been renaming by hand and last month I clobbered a card doing it: I renamed 01 onto 02 before moving 02 out of the way and ate a photo. Never again. I want a proper tool: `renum.sh`, repo root, plain bash, and it must run on the archive's old Mac mini too, so portable commands only. Pin LC_ALL=C inside the script — ordering must never depend on who runs it.

Usage: `renum.sh [--dry-run] [--start N] [--width W] <dir> <prefix>` (flags anywhere before/among/after the positionals is fine, but exactly two positionals).

The batch is every regular file directly inside <dir> — no recursion, dotfiles and subdirectories are left alone entirely. Files are processed in C byte order of their current names. Each gets the new name `<prefix><number>` plus its extension: if the old name contains a dot, the extension is whatever follows the LAST dot, kept verbatim (`archive.tar.gz` becomes `<prefix><n>.gz`, that's fine, don't get clever); a name with no dot gets no extension. Numbers start at --start (default 1) and count up by one per file. Zero-padding width: --width if given, otherwise just wide enough for the largest number in the batch (digits of start+count-1) but never less than 2 — so 8 files from 1 are 01..08, and 3 files from 998 are 0998, 0999, 1000. A --width smaller than the largest number needs is an error: `renum.sh: --width too small: need <D> digit(s)` to stderr, exit 65.

If a file's computed target equals its current name it is UNCHANGED — skipped, no rename, which is what makes re-running the tool on an already-numbered directory a no-op that only picks up new arrivals.

Safety, the whole reason this tool exists: renames must survive overlap between old and new names. `--start 2` over shot-01/shot-02/shot-03 means 01->02, 02->03, 03->04, and every byte must end up under the right final name — do it in two phases (park everything that moves under temp names first, then settle them into finals) or any other scheme that provably cannot eat a file. And before touching ANYTHING: if some target name already exists in the directory but is NOT one of the batch files (a subdirectory with that name, say), refuse the whole job — `renum.sh: target exists outside the batch: <name>` to stderr, exit 65, directory left exactly as found.

`--dry-run` prints the plan and changes nothing: one line per planned rename, `<old> -> <new>` (spaces around the arrow), in processing order, then `plan: <K> rename(s), <M> unchanged`. A real run prints only `renamed: <K> file(s), <M> unchanged` on success. Errors: bad invocation (wrong positional count, empty prefix, unknown flag, missing value, --start/--width not a positive integer) prints `usage: renum.sh [--dry-run] [--start N] [--width W] <dir> <prefix>` to stderr, exit 64; <dir> missing or not a directory is `renum.sh: not a directory: <arg>`, exit 66; a directory with no regular files is `renum.sh: no regular files in: <dir>`, exit 65. Success prints nothing to stderr.

Acceptance is `bash test_renum.sh` from the workspace root, unmodified — don't touch the test file.

checks=0

assert_eq() { # assert_eq <label> <expected> <actual>
  checks=$((checks + 1))
  if [[ "$2" == "$3" ]]; then
    printf 'PASS %s\n' "$1"
    return 0
  fi
  fails=$((fails + 1))
  printf 'FAIL %s\n--- expected ---\n%s\n--- actual ---\n%s\n----------------\n' "$1" "$2" "$3"

}

assert_content() { # assert_content <label> <file> <expected-one-line-content>
  checks=$((checks + 1))

    IFS= read -r got < "$2" || true

TASK
I run the scan station for the county archive digitization project. Every batch lands as a directory of files with whatever names the scanner and the volunteers' cameras invented — `IMG 0007.JPG`, `clip.mov`, bare `notes` — and before ingest they all have to follow our sequence scheme. I've been renaming by hand and last month I clobbered a card doing it: I renamed 01 onto 02 before moving 02 out of the way and ate a photo. Never again. I want a proper tool: `renum.sh`, repo root, plain bash, and it must run on the archive's old Mac mini too, so portable commands only. Pin LC_ALL=C inside the script — ordering must never depend on who runs it.

Usage: `renum.sh [--dry-run] [--start N] [--width W] <dir> <prefix>` (flags anywhere before/among/after the positionals is fine, but exactly two positionals).

The batch is every regular file directly inside <dir> — no recursion, dotfiles and subdirectories are left alone entirely. Files are processed in C byte order of their current names. Each gets the new name `<prefix><number>` plus its extension: if the old name contains a dot, the extension is whatever follows the LAST dot, kept verbatim (`archive.tar.gz` becomes `<prefix><n>.gz`, that's fine, don't get clever); a name with no dot gets no extension. Numbers start at --start (default 1) and count up by one per file. Zero-padding width: --width if given, otherwise just wide enough for the largest number in the batch (digits of start+count-1) but never less than 2 — so 8 files from 1 are 01..08, and 3 files from 998 are 0998, 0999, 1000. A --width smaller than the largest number needs is an error: `renum.sh: --width too small: need <D> digit(s)` to stderr, exit 65.

If a file's computed target equals its current name it is UNCHANGED — skipped, no rename, which is what makes re-running the tool on an already-numbered directory a no-op that only picks up new arrivals.

Safety, the whole reason this tool exists: renames must survive overlap between old and new names. `--start 2` over shot-01/shot-02/shot-03 means 01->02, 02->03, 03->04, and every byte must end up under the right final name — do it in two phases (park everything that moves under temp names first, then settle them into finals) or any other scheme that provably cannot eat a file. And before touching ANYTHING: if some target name already exists in the directory but is NOT one of the batch files (a subdirectory with that name, say), refuse the whole job — `renum.sh: target exists outside the batch: <name>` to stderr, exit 65, directory left exactly as found.

`--dry-run` prints the plan and changes nothing: one line per planned rename, `<old> -> <new>` (spaces around the arrow), in processing order, then `plan: <K> rename(s), <M> unchanged`. A real run prints only `renamed: <K> file(s), <M> unchanged` on success. Errors: bad invocation (wrong positional count, empty prefix, unknown flag, missing value, --start/--width not a positive integer) prints `usage: renum.sh [--dry-run] [--start N] [--width W] <dir> <prefix>` to stderr, exit 64; <dir> missing or not a directory is `renum.sh: not a directory: <arg>`, exit 66; a directory with no regular files is `renum.sh: no regular files in: <dir>`, exit 65. Testing our retry/heartbeat logic against real setTimeout has made the CI suite both slow AND flaky, so I want a deterministic scheduler we fully control. scheduler.ts, export class VirtualScheduler. No real timers anywhere in it — time only moves when the caller says so.

API + semantics (test_scheduler.ts is the source of truth, `node --test test_scheduler.ts`):
- now(): current virtual ms, starts at 0
- schedule(fn, delayMs): one-shot, returns an id. delayMs < 0 is a RangeError; 0 is fine and fires on the next advance, even advance(0)
- scheduleRepeating(fn, intervalMs): fires at every exact multiple of intervalMs from when it was scheduled — drift-free, meaning one advance(35) with interval 10 fires at t=10, 20, 30 (three times), and the NEXT fire is still t=40, no matter how ragged the advances were. intervalMs <= 0 is a RangeError
- cancel(id): true if it cancelled something pending, false otherwise; works for both kinds; cancelling from inside a callback must stop a not-yet-run task even at the same timestamp
- advance(ms): runs everything due in (now, now+ms], strictly in fire-time order, FIFO for ties; inside a callback now() reports that callback's scheduled fire time, not the advance target; tasks a callback schedules during the advance also run if they land inside the window; afterwards now() is the advance target
- advanceTo(t): absolute-time sugar for the same thing
- pending(): count of live scheduled tasks (a repeater counts once)

One more thing that bit us with our homegrown attempt: if a callback throws, let the exception surface out of advance() — but don't corrupt the scheduler. now() should sit at the failed task's fire time and everything still queued must run on a later advance.

The perf suite budgets the cumulative reported total at 6x the final sheet length for the 150k-row export, so anything that keeps re-copying its buffer can't pass.

node --test test_tally.ts is the acceptance contract — don't touch the test file.

Cleanup ticket on roster.ts, our newsletter-roster client. It's 2020-style promise chains, and every method resolves to a { ok, ... } result object that never rejects. In practice that's been a bug factory: three incidents this year were callers reading .data off a result they never checked, and TypeScript can't save them because everything is behind that union. We're standardizing on async/await plus thrown typed errors across the codebase, and roster.ts is next.

What I want in the same file: a RosterClient class constructed with the same injected transport (don't change the transport contract — the CLI and the tests hand one in), async methods getSubscriber(id), subscribe(email, name), unsubscribe(id). Success now resolves straight to the payload (unsubscribe resolves to null), failure THROWS. Error taxonomy: a RosterError base class with a .code, and subclasses NotFoundError, AlreadySubscribedError (carries .email), ValidationError (carries .fields), RateLimitError (carries .retryAfterSeconds), NetworkError for transport rejections (original error attached as .cause). Unexpected statuses throw the base RosterError itself with code 'api'. Each class sets .name to its class name.

Two things must not drift. First, the wire behavior: identical requests, identical status handling. Second, the error MESSAGE strings: they must be byte-identical to what the old result objects carried ('subscriber s_9 not found', 'rate limited, retry in 30s', etc.) because the on-call dashboards grep logs for those exact phrases. The result-object shape itself is dead — nothing should resolve with an ok flag ever again. test_roster.ts pins all of this; run node --test test_roster.ts and leave the test file alone.

From the pottery studio's slack, #kiln-controller channel. The controller keeps 'forgetting' our firing profile between sessions and it's ruining loads. Saturday we dialed in the slow bisque — ramp 120, target 2232, hold 25 — hit save, fired, everything perfect. Sunday morning after the controller's nightly restart it ramped at the factory 150 again and the display said profile 'bisque-04' like we'd never touched it. No error on the panel, no error in the log. The profile file on disk is RIGHT — I can literally cat it and see ramp_rate 120 in the JSON. It saves fine. It just comes back from a restart acting like the factory profile.

Two more data points from this weekend. The quiet-hours window we set (21:00 to 05:30, so the horn doesn't wake the neighbors) also reverts to 22:00/06:00 after every restart, same silent way. And here's the kicker: if you fix one dial after a restart and save — say you re-set the hold time — the NEXT restart keeps your hold time but the ramp and target you'd saved before quietly revert to factory. It's like every save after a restart slowly shreds the profile.

While the controller stays up, everything behaves: tweaks apply, save writes the file, to_h shows the right numbers. Only restarts (save then load) misbehave.

The controller piece is FiringConfig in firing_config.rb, right here. Find it and fix it — small fix, no API changes, the on-disk file stays JSON. test_firing_config.rb is the acceptance contract; hands off the test file. Done when `ruby test_firing_config.rb` passes.

require "json"

# Firing profile for the studio's kiln controller. The panel edits one
# profile in memory; between sessions it lives as a JSON file next to the
# controller state. All programmatic access uses symbol keys.
class FiringConfig
  DEFAULTS = {
    profile_name: "bisque-04",
    ramp_rate: 150,      # degrees F per hour
    target_temp: 1945,   # cone 04
    hold_minutes: 10,
    quiet_hours: { start: "22:00", stop: "06:00" } # no alarm horn in this window
  }.freeze

  def initialize(overrides = {})
    @settings = {}
    overrides.each { |key, value| set(key, value) }
  end

  # Panel dial writes land here.
  def set(key, value)
    raise ArgumentError, "unknown setting #{key.inspect}" unless DEFAULTS.key?(key)

    @settings[key] = value
    self
  end

  def profile_name = lookup(:profile_name)
  def ramp_rate    = lookup(:ramp_rate)
  def target_temp  = lookup(:target_temp)
  def hold_minutes = lookup(:hold_minutes)

  def quiet_start = lookup(:quiet_hours)[:start]
  def quiet_stop  = lookup(:quiet_hours)[:stop]

  # Effective settings: factory values overlaid with this profile's tweaks.
  def to_h
    DEFAULTS.merge(@settings)
  end

  def save(path)
    File.write(path, JSON.generate(@settings))
    path
  end

  def self.load(path)
    config = new
    config.restore(JSON.parse(File.read(path)))
    config
  end

  # Used by load and by the controller's crash-recovery path.
  def restore(data)
    @settings = data
    self
  end

  private

  def lookup(key)
    @settings.key?(key) ? @settings[key] : DEFAULTS[key]
  end
end

require "minitest/autorun"
require "fileutils"
require "json"
require_relative "firing_config"

# Contract tests for the kiln controller's firing profile: panel edits,
# persistence across controller restarts (save -> load), effective settings.
class FiringConfigTest < Minitest::Test
  SCRATCH = File.join(Dir.pwd, "kiln_scratch")

  def setup
    FileUtils.mkdir_p(SCRATCH)
    @path = File.join(SCRATCH, "evening-glaze.json")
  end

  def teardown
    FileUtils.rm_rf(SCRATCH)
  end

  def test_factory_defaults_apply_out_of_the_box
    config = FiringConfig.new
    assert_equal "bisque-04", config.profile_name
    assert_equal 150, config.ramp_rate
    assert_equal 1945, config.target_temp
    assert_equal 10, config.hold_minutes
    assert_equal "22:00", config.quiet_start
    assert_equal "06:00", config.quiet_stop
  end

  def test_panel_tweaks_take_effect_immediately
    config = FiringConfig.new(ramp_rate: 120, target_temp: 2232)
    assert_equal 120, config.ramp_rate
    assert_equal 2232, config.target_temp
    config.set(:hold_minutes, 25)
    assert_equal 25, config.hold_minutes
    config.set(:quiet_hours, { start: "21:00", stop: "05:30" })
    assert_equal "21:00", config.quiet_start
  end

  def test_unknown_settings_are_rejected
    err = assert_raises(ArgumentError) { FiringConfig.new.set(:rampratee, 100) }
    assert_equal "unknown setting :rampratee", err.message
  end

  def test_save_writes_the_profile_as_json
    FiringConfig.new(ramp_rate: 120).save(@path)
    raw = JSON.parse(File.read(@path))
    assert_equal 120, raw["ramp_rate"]
  end

  def test_a_saved_profile_survives_a_controller_restart
    config = FiringConfig.new(profile_name: "evening-glaze", ramp_rate: 120, target_temp: 2232)
    config.save(@path)
    back = FiringConfig.load(@path)
    assert_equal 120, back.ramp_rate
    assert_equal 2232, back.target_temp
    assert_equal "evening-glaze", back.profile_name
    assert_equal 10, back.hold_minutes
  end

  def test_quiet_hours_survive_a_controller_restart
    config = FiringConfig.new(quiet_hours: { start: "21:00", stop: "05:30" })
    config.save(@path)
    back = FiringConfig.load(@path)
    assert_equal "21:00", back.quiet_start
    assert_equal "05:30", back.quiet_stop
  end

  def test_a_tweak_after_a_restart_keeps_the_earlier_tweaks
    FiringConfig.new(ramp_rate: 120, target_temp: 2232).save(@path)
    session_two = FiringConfig.load(@path)
    session_two.set(:hold_minutes, 25)
    session_two.save(@path)
    session_three = FiringConfig.load(@path)
    assert_equal 25, session_three.hold_minutes
    assert_equal 120, session_three.ramp_rate
    assert_equal 2232, session_three.target_temp
  end

  def test_effective_settings_list_each_setting_exactly_once_after_a_restart
    FiringConfig.new(ramp_rate: 120).save(@path)
    effective = FiringConfig.load(@path).to_h
    assert_equal 5, effective.size
    assert_equal FiringConfig::DEFAULTS.keys.sort, effective.keys.sort
    assert_equal 120, effective[:ramp_rate]
    assert_equal 1945, effective[:target_temp]
  end
end

require "json"

# Firing profile for the studio's kiln controller. The panel edits one
# profile in memory; between sessions it lives as a JSON file next to the
# controller state. All programmatic access uses symbol keys.
class FiringConfig
  DEFAULTS = {
    profile_name: "bisque-04",
    ramp_rate: 150,      # degrees F per hour
    target_temp: 1945,   # cone 04
    hold_minutes: 10,
    quiet_hours: { start: "22:00", stop: "06:00" } # no alarm horn in this window
  }.freeze

  def initialize(overrides = {})
    @settings = {}
    overrides.each { |key, value| set(key, value) }
  end

  # Panel dial writes land here.
  def set(key, value)
    raise ArgumentError, "unknown setting #{key.inspect}" unless DEFAULTS.key?(key)

    @settings[key] = value
    self
  end

  def profile_name = lookup(:profile_name)
  def ramp_rate    = lookup(:ramp_rate)
  def target_temp  = lookup(:target_temp)
  def hold_minutes = lookup(:hold_minutes)

  def quiet_start = lookup(:quiet_hours)[:start]
  def quiet_stop  = lookup(:quiet_hours)[:stop]

  # Effective settings: factory values overlaid with this profile's tweaks.
  def to_h
    DEFAULTS.merge(@settings)
  end

  def save(path)
    File.write(path, JSON.generate(@settings))
    path
  end

  def self.load(path)
    config = new
    config.restore(JSON.parse(File.read(path)))
    config
  end

  # Used by load and by the controller's crash-recovery path.
  def restore(data)
    @settings = data
    self
  end

  private

  def lookup(key)
    @settings.key?(key) ? @settings[key] : DEFAULTS[key]
  end
end

require "json"

# Firing profile for the studio's kiln controller. The panel edits one
# profile in memory; between sessions it lives as a JSON file next to the
# controller state. All programmatic access uses symbol keys.
class FiringConfig
  DEFAULTS = {
    profile_name: "bisque-04",
    ramp_rate: 150,      # degrees F per hour
    target_temp: 1945,   # cone 04
    hold_minutes: 10,
    quiet_hours: { start: "22:00", stop: "06:00" } # no alarm horn in this window
  }.freeze

  def initialize(overrides = {})
    @settings = {}
    overrides.each { |key, value| set(key, value) }
  end

  # Panel dial writes land here.
  def set(key, value)
    raise ArgumentError, "unknown setting #{key.inspect}" unless DEFAULTS.key?(key)

    @settings[key] = value
    self
  end

  def profile_name = lookup(:profile_name)
  def ramp_rate    = lookup(:ramp_rate)
  def target_temp  = lookup(:target_temp)
  def hold_minutes = lookup(:hold_minutes)

  def quiet_start = lookup(:quiet_hours)[:start]
  def quiet_stop  = lookup(:quiet_hours)[:stop]

  # Effective settings: factory values overlaid with this profile's tweaks.
  def to_h
    DEFAULTS.merge(@settings)
  end

  def save(path)
    File.write(path, JSON.generate(@settings))
    path
  end

  def self.load(path)
    config = new
    config.restore(JSON.parse(File.read(path)))
    config
  end

  # Used by load and by the controller's crash-recovery path.
  def restore(data)
    @settings = data
    self
  end

  private

  def lookup(key)
    @settings.key?(key) ? @settings[key] : DEFAULTS[key]
  end
end

state:
TASK
Need a small open-addressing hash map in C for the stockroom snapshot tool, and I am going to be opinionated about the internals, because we diff textual dumps of this table between runs and between machines — the layout has to be byte-for-byte reproducible, not "whatever the implementation felt like". Two new files: hs.h and hs.c. C17, stdlib only.

API (exact — the dump tool and the tests are already written against it):

    typedef struct hs_map hs_map;    /* opaque; definition lives in hs.c */

    hs_map *hs_new(void);                                  /* NULL on alloc failure */
    void    hs_free(hs_map *m);                            /* frees key copies, table, map */
    int     hs_put(hs_map *m, const char *key, void *val); /* 0 ok; -1 alloc failure */
    void   *hs_get(const hs_map *m, const char *key);      /* NULL if absent */
    int     hs_del(hs_map *m, const char *key);            /* 0 removed; -1 absent */
    size_t  hs_len(const hs_map *m);                       /* live entries */
    size_t  hs_cap(const hs_map *m);                       /* slot count */
    int     hs_next(const hs_map *m, size_t *it, const char **key, void **val);

Layout policy, pinned exactly:

- Hash: FNV-1a, 32-bit. Start h = 2166136261; for each byte of the key: h ^= byte, then h *= 16777619, wrapping at 32 bits (use uint32_t). Hash the key bytes only, no terminator.
- Capacity is always a power of two, starting at 16. Home slot = h & (cap - 1). Collisions probe linearly: +1, wrapping.
- Deletion leaves a tombstone: the slot is neither empty nor live. Lookups treat tombstones as "keep probing"; only a truly empty slot ends a probe.
- hs_put probes for the key first. Found -> replace the value in place (len unchanged, the existing key copy is kept). Not found -> it's an insert: if (used + 1) * 10 > cap * 7, where used counts live entries PLUS tombstones, rehash into a table of DOUBLE the capacity before placing. Rehash walks the old table in slot order (ascending index), re-inserts live entries into the new table (fresh probe, no load check), and drops tombstones. After any needed rehash, the new entry goes into the first tombstone its probe passed, if any (that slot flips back to live; used stays the same), otherwise into the empty slot that ended the probe (used grows by one).
- hs_next is a cursor iterator: size_t it = 0; while (hs_next(m, &it, &k, &v)) ... yields every live entry in ascending slot order — i.e. iteration order IS the probe-sequence layout. Returns 0 when done. No modification during iteration; I don't need that and won't defend it.

Ownership: hs_put copies the key (map owns the copies and frees them on hs_del/hs_free; hs_next hands back pointers to the map's own copies — caller must not free or hold them past the next mutation). Values are opaque void* owned by the caller; the map never touches what they point at.

Why so rigid: with these rules two boxes that apply the same operations end up with identical tables, so our snapshot diffs only ever show real changes. The tests encode exact iteration sequences for fixed key sets (including a chain of colliding part names, a deleted-slot reuse, and both rehash triggers — the plain twelfth-key one and the one where tombstones push occupancy over the line). If your layout differs from the policy above, the diffs light up and the tests will tell you.

`make test` from the repo root is the acceptance gate. Makefile, mintest.h, test_hs.c are fixed — don't edit them.

state:
TASK
So the story: we shard session blobs across a fleet of cache hosts with `hash(key) % len(hosts)`, and every time autoscaling adds or drains a host basically EVERY key remaps and the origin gets stampeded. Friday's incident was exactly this. I've been told 'just use consistent hashing' in three separate retros now, so here we are — and I don't want a dependency, I want it in-tree where I can read it.

Package ring, root of module go-hashring. Surface:

  func New(virtualNodes int) (*Ring, error)
  func (r *Ring) AddNode(name string) error
  func (r *Ring) RemoveNode(name string) error
  func (r *Ring) Get(key string) (string, error)
  func (r *Ring) Nodes() []string
  var ErrEmptyRing, ErrNodeExists, ErrUnknownNode

Requirements, in my words:
- virtualNodes is replicas-per-node on the ring, must be >= 1 or New errors. More vnodes = smoother spread; with 128 vnodes and 3 nodes the split should be roughly even, and the suite checks that.
- Get maps a key to a node name. Empty ring -> ErrEmptyRing. AddNode on a name already present -> ErrNodeExists; RemoveNode on a name that isn't there -> ErrUnknownNode; and a failed call must not perturb placement at all.
- Placement must be a pure function of current membership: same nodes = same answers, regardless of what order they were added in, and remove-then-re-add restores the exact old mapping. That means deterministic hashing, no seeds, no map-iteration-order leakage. Pick something from the stdlib that actually disperses — node labels and keys are short near-identical strings ('shard-0', 'session:00042'), and the weaker string hashes visibly clump on those.
- THE point of all this, the property that fixes Friday: removing a node may only move keys that lived on that node, and adding a node may only move keys onto the new node. Everything else stays put.
- Nodes() returns current members sorted lexicographically, fresh slice each call.

Stdlib only. ring_test.go is the contract — hands off. Green under go test -race -timeout 30s ./... and I'll believe it.

state:
TASK
Perf ticket from the observability side. stitch.ts folds the gateway's audit-log stream (one 'open' entry and one 'close' entry per RPC, keyed by call id) back into call records for the latency dashboard. On staging traffic it was fine; on a production day (~160k entries) the stitch job pegs a core for ages and the dashboard misses its refresh window. The reason is plain once you watch it: every time a close comes in, the resolver walks back through the stored open log entry by entry until it finds the right open — the longer the day, the longer every walk.

Speed it up without moving the semantics one inch. Contract (also documented in the module header): a close consumes the MOST RECENT still-unconsumed open with its id — same-id opens nest like a stack, our retries depend on that; calls come out in close order with { id, method, openTs, closeTs, durationMs, status } and durationMs = closeTs - openTs; unmatchedOpens holds ids of never-consumed opens in open order; orphanCloses holds closes that found nothing, in close order. Output order is load-bearing — downstream diffs snapshots.

Keep the stitch(entries, opts) signature and keep the probe accounting honest: onProbe(candidate.id) must still fire once for every stored open entry you examine while resolving a close. The perf suite budgets total probes at 3x the entry count for the 160k-entry day, so per-close rescans of the log can't pass; examining just the open you actually consume is obviously fine.

node --test test_stitch.ts is the acceptance contract — leave the test file alone.

state:
TASK
Telemetry-ingest ticket. Our batch scorer walks a slice of readings, maps each fixed-size chunk to a partial result on a worker thread, and merges the partials. The prototype wrapped everything in Arc<Vec<T>> and cloned readings into each worker, which (a) forced T: Clone onto callers that don't have it and (b) made results own copies when callers want to hand back references INTO the input (e.g. "the max element"). Rust has had std::thread::scope since 1.63 — workers can borrow the slice directly. Rewrite it that way.

This crate is rs-scopedproc (lib name rs_scopedproc, Cargo.toml already in place — leave it and .gitignore alone). Stdlib only, no unsafe, no Arc anywhere in this feature. Everything in src/. The acceptance contract is tests/scopedproc.rs, byte for byte as checked in: `cargo test --offline` fully green, test file untouched.

Public API, exactly one function plus its error enum:

- `pub enum ChunkError { ZeroChunkSize, ZeroWorkers }` — derive Debug, PartialEq, Eq.
- `pub fn process_chunks<'a, T, R, M, G>(items: &'a [T], chunk_size: usize, workers: usize, map_fn: M, merge_fn: G) -> Result<Option<R>, ChunkError>` where `T: Sync`, `R: Send`, `M: Fn(usize, &'a [T]) -> R + Sync`, `G: FnMut(R, R) -> R`. Note the lifetimes: map results may borrow from `items` (the contract asserts pointer identity on a returned `&u32`), so the map closure takes `&'a [T]`, not a higher-ranked borrow.

Semantics, exactly as the tests pin them:

- Validate first, in this order: chunk_size == 0 is ZeroChunkSize, then workers == 0 is ZeroWorkers — BOTH checked before the empty-input shortcut, so garbage arguments never pass just because the slice was empty.
- Empty input: Ok(None), and map_fn must never run.
- Chunking: contiguous, in order, chunk i covers items[i*chunk_size ..], last chunk ragged. map_fn receives (chunk_index, sub-slice).
- Assignment is round-robin over min(workers, number_of_chunks) scoped worker threads: worker w owns chunks w, w+n, w+2n, ... and processes its own chunks in ascending index order. Spawn only that many threads — 16 requested workers over 3 chunks means exactly 3 worker threads.
- Merge happens on the calling thread after the workers are done, as a LEFT FOLD in chunk-index order: (((r0 merge r1) merge r2) merge r3) — regardless of which worker finished first. The contract includes a channel-gated test where chunk 0 provably finishes after chunk 1; completion order must not leak into the merge.
- Workers borrow the input; nothing is cloned. T carries no Clone/Default bounds and one test uses a deliberately non-Clone struct.

Don't add public API beyond these two items, don't sleep or poll anywhere, and don't fall back to processing on the caller thread when workers >= 1 (the gate test deadlocks any sequential implementation and its 10-second backstop will name the bug). Same input must produce byte-identical output on every run — the fold order guarantees that for free if you implement it as specified.

state:
TASK
Ticket from the edge-runtime team. Our agent needs a tiny embedded KV store for its config cache — bolt/badger are overkill and the edge builds are stdlib-only. Module go-kvwal, package kvwal, this repo.

Storage model: exactly one append-only write-ahead log at <dir>/wal.log. Every mutation appends a record; the in-memory map is rebuilt by replaying the log on Open. The on-disk framing is fixed because the recovery tests poke at the file directly: each record is a 4-byte big-endian payload length, then a 4-byte big-endian IEEE CRC32 of the payload, then the payload bytes. What goes inside the payload (op tag, key/value encoding) is your design.

API:
- Open(dir string) (*Store, error) — creates wal.log if missing, replays it otherwise. If the tail is torn or garbage (declared length runs past EOF, CRC mismatch, or the payload won't decode), keep every record before the bad one, truncate the file to that valid prefix right there in Open, and carry on. A writer that died mid-append must never brick the store.
- Put(key string, value []byte) error — empty key is an error and stores nothing. Overwrite = append a new record; last record for a key wins on replay. Defensive copies both ways: a caller reusing its value buffer, or scribbling on a slice Get returned, must not corrupt the store.
- Get(key string) ([]byte, bool). Zero-length values are legal and distinct from missing.
- Delete(key string) error — appends a tombstone; the key stays dead across reopens. Deleting a missing key is a no-op, not an error. A Put after a tombstone resurrects the key.
- Keys() []string (live keys, sorted ascending) and Len() int (live key count).
- Compact() error — rewrite the log to just the live state (no tombstones, no superseded versions) and swap it in atomically: build a temp file, rename it over wal.log, never leave a half-written log as the real one. Appends must keep working after a compact.
- Close() error — Put/Delete/Compact after Close return errors.

The store is hit from multiple goroutines and CI runs -race, so make it safe. kvwal_test.go and recovery_test.go are the acceptance contract — do not touch them; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass. Structure it like a real package: store logic, record encode/replay, and compaction in separate files, not one giant blob.

TASK
Ticket from the edge-runtime team. Our agent needs a tiny embedded KV store for its config cache — bolt/badger are overkill and the edge builds are stdlib-only. Module go-kvwal, package kvwal, this repo.

Storage model: exactly one append-only write-ahead log at <dir>/wal.log. Every mutation appends a record; the in-memory map is rebuilt by replaying the log on Open. The on-disk framing is fixed because the recovery tests poke at the file directly: each record is a 4-byte big-endian payload length, then a 4-byte big-endian IEEE CRC32 of the payload, then the payload bytes. What goes inside the payload (op tag, key/value encoding) is your design.

API:
- Open(dir string) (*Store, error) — creates wal.log if missing, replays it otherwise. If the tail is torn or garbage (declared length runs past EOF, CRC mismatch, or the payload won't decode), keep every record before the bad one, truncate the file to that valid prefix right there in Open, and carry on. A writer that died mid-append must never brick the store.
- Put(key string, value []byte) error — empty key is an error and stores nothing. Overwrite = append a new record; last record for a key wins on replay. Defensive copies both ways: a caller reusing its value buffer, or scribbling on a slice Get returned, must not corrupt the store.
- Get(key string) ([]byte, bool). Zero-length values are legal and distinct from missing.
- Delete(key string) error — appends a tombstone; the key stays dead across reopens. Deleting a missing key is a no-op, not an error. A Put after a tombstone resurrects the key.
- Keys() []string (live keys, sorted ascending) and Len() int (live key count).
- Compact() error — rewrite the log to just the live state (no tombstones, no superseded versions) and swap it in atomically: build a temp file, rename it over wal.log, never leave a half-written log as the real one. Appends must keep working after a compact.
- Close() error — Put/Delete/Compact after Close return errors.

The store is hit from multiple goroutines and CI runs -race, so make it safe. kvwal_test.go and recovery_test.go are the acceptance contract — do not touch them; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass. Structure it like a real package: store logic, record encode/replay, and compaction in separate files, not one giant blob.

func walPath(dir string) string { return filepath.Join(dir, "wal.log") }

func fileSize(t *testing.T, path string) int64 {
	t.Helper()
	fi, err := os.Stat(path)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("stat %s: %v", path, err)
	}
	return fi.Size()
}

	dir := t.TempDir()
	st := openStore(t, dir)
	mustPut(t, st, "alpha", []byte("survives"))
	mustPut(t, st, "omega", []byte("torn away"))
	mustClose(t, st)

	// Simulate a crash mid-append: the last record loses its final bytes.
	size := fileSize(t, walPath(dir))
	if err := os.Truncate(walPath(dir), size-3); err != nil {

}
