TASK
Calder Street depot, maintenance desk app. Two complaints from the shop floor this week; both reproduce on a clean checkout with `ruby test_fleetdesk.rb` (that suite is the acceptance bar and is read-only).

1) The wall display's shop dashboard freezes on wrench time. Yesterday: one open work order on the box truck, dashboard showing labor_minutes 0. The mechanic booked 45 minutes (front pads) and then another 30 - the order itself is fine, reading it back shows 75 minutes and both log entries. The dashboard kept saying 0. It sat at 0 until the desk did something else entirely (opened another order), at which point it jumped straight to 75. Parts do NOT behave this way: booking a $125.00 part (we store cents, so 12500) shows on the dashboard immediately. Closing an order updates it immediately too. It is specifically labor that lags, every time, until some other kind of desk action happens.

2) The mechanics' board URL is dead. The documented endpoint is GET /work_orders/board and the kiosk front end was just repointed to it, but it comes back 404 with {error: "no such work order: board"} - the app is apparently reading 'board' as an order number. Meanwhile the OLD path from two front-end versions ago, GET /work_orders/queue, still returns the board fine, which is why the shop's stale kiosk bookmarks keep working. queue was supposed to be retired in that same update; board is the one that must live.

Might be one bug, might be two. Work out what is actually wrong and fix the app - and do not touch test_fleetdesk.rb.

module FleetDesk
  # Wires the depot desk together and dispatches requests. The kiosk front
  # end calls App#call with (verb, path, params) triples.
  class App
    def initialize
      store = Store::MemoryStore.new
      vehicles = Store::VehicleRepo.new(store)
      orders = Store::OrderRepo.new(store)

      reports = Services::ReportService.new(orders, vehicles)
      vehicle_service = Services::VehicleService.new(vehicles, orders)
      work_order_service = Services::WorkOrderService.new(orders, vehicles, reports)

      @router = Router.new
      Routes::Vehicles.register(@router, vehicle_service)
      Routes::WorkOrders.register(@router, work_order_service)
      Routes::Reports.register(@router, reports)
    end

    def call(verb, path, params = {})
      verb = verb.to_s.upcase
      hit = @router.match(verb, path)
      return Response.not_found("no route: #{verb} #{path}") unless hit

      handler, path_params = hit
      request = Request.new(verb, path, params.merge(path_params))
      handler.call(request)
    rescue Services::NotFound => e
      Response.not_found(e.message)
    rescue ArgumentError => e
      Response.unprocessable(e.message)
    end
  end
end

module FleetDesk
  # Tiny first-match-wins route table. Path patterns are literal segments
  # or :captures ("/work_orders/:id"); no globs, no regexps.
  class Router
    Route = Struct.new(:verb, :segments, :handler)

    def initialize
      @routes = []
    end

    def get(path, &handler)
      add("GET", path, handler)
    end

    def post(path, &handler)
      add("POST", path, handler)
    end

    # [handler, captured params] for the first route that matches, else nil.
    def match(verb, path)
      parts = split(path)
      @routes.each do |route|
        next unless route.verb == verb

        params = match_segments(route.segments, parts)
        return [route.handler, params] if params
      end
      nil
    end

    private

    def add(verb, path, handler)
      @routes << Route.new(verb, split(path), handler)
    end

    def split(path)
      path.split("/").reject(&:empty?)
    end

    def match_segments(pattern, parts)
      return nil unless pattern.length == parts.length

      params = {}
      pattern.zip(parts) do |expected, actual|
        if expected.start_with?(":")
          params[expected[1..].to_sym] = actual
        elsif expected != actual
          return nil
        end
      end
      params
    end
  end
end

module FleetDesk
  # Wires the depot desk together and dispatches requests. The kiosk front
  # end calls App#call with (verb, path, params) triples.
  class App
    def initialize
      store = Store::MemoryStore.new
      vehicles = Store::VehicleRepo.new(store)
      orders = Store::OrderRepo.new(store)

      reports = Services::ReportService.new(orders, vehicles)
      vehicle_service = Services::VehicleService.new(vehicles, orders)
      work_order_service = Services::WorkOrderService.new(orders, vehicles, reports)

      @router = Router.new
      Routes::Vehicles.register(@router, vehicle_service)
      Routes::WorkOrders.register(@router, work_order_service)
      Routes::Reports.register(@router, reports)
    end

    def call(verb, path, params = {})
      verb = verb.to_s.upcase
      hit = @router.match(verb, path)
      return Response.not_found("no route: #{verb} #{path}") unless hit

      handler, path_params = hit
      request = Request.new(verb, path, params.merge(path_params))
      handler.call(request)
    rescue Services::NotFound => e
      Response.not_found(e.message)
    rescue ArgumentError => e
      Response.unprocessable(e.message)
    end
  end
end

module FleetDesk
  # Tiny first-match-wins route table. Path patterns are literal segments
  # or :captures ("/work_orders/:id"); no globs, no regexps.
  class Router
    Route = Struct.new(:verb, :segments, :handler)

    def initialize
      @routes = []
    end

    def get(path, &handler)
      add("GET", path, handler)
    end

    def post(path, &handler)
      add("POST", path, handler)
    end

    # [handler, captured params] for the first route that matches, else nil.
    def match(verb, path)
      parts = split(path)
      @routes.each do |route|
        next unless route.verb == verb

        params = match_segments(route.segments, parts)
        return [route.handler, params] if params
      end
      nil
    end

    private

    def add(verb, path, handler)
      @routes << Route.new(verb, split(path), handler)
    end

    def split(path)
      path.split("/").reject(&:empty?)
    end

    def match_segments(pattern, parts)
      return nil unless pattern.length == parts.length

      params = {}
      pattern.zip(parts) do |expected, actual|
        if expected.start_with?(":")
          params[expected[1..].to_sym] = actual
        elsif expected != actual
          return nil
        end
      end
      params
    end
  end
end

module FleetDesk
  module Services
    # Work orders: opening jobs against a vehicle, booking labor and parts,
    # closing out, and the mechanics' board of open jobs.
    class WorkOrderService
      def initialize(orders, vehicles, reports)
        @orders = orders
        @vehicles = vehicles
        @reports = reports
      end

      def open_order(unit:, task:)
        raise NotFound, "no vehicle with unit #{unit}" unless @vehicles.exists?(unit)
        raise ArgumentError, "task must not be blank" if task.nil? || task.strip.empty?

        order = @orders.insert(
          unit: unit,
          task: task,
          status: "open",
          labor_minutes: 0,
          parts_cents: 0,
          labor_log: [],
          parts: []
        )
        @reports.invalidate
        order
      end

      def log_labor(id, minutes:, note: nil)
        order = require_open(id)
        unless minutes.is_a?(Integer) && minutes > 0
          raise ArgumentError, "minutes must be a positive integer"
        end

        order[:labor_minutes] += minutes
        order[:labor_log] << { minutes: minutes, note: note }
        @orders.update(order)
        order
      end

      def add_part(id, item:, cents:)
        order = require_open(id)
        raise ArgumentError, "item must not be blank" if item.nil? || item.strip.empty?
        unless cents.is_a?(Integer) && cents > 0
          raise ArgumentError, "cents must be a positive integer"
        end

        order[:parts_cents] += cents
        order[:parts] << { item: item, cents: cents }
        @orders.update(order)
        @reports.invalidate
        order
      end

      def close_order(id)
        order = require_open(id)
        order[:status] = "closed"
        @orders.update(order)
        @reports.invalidate
        order
      end

      def fetch(id)
        @orders.find(id) or raise NotFound, "no such work order: #{id}"
      end

      # Open jobs for the mechanics' board, oldest first.
      def board
        @orders.all.select { |order| order[:status] == "open" }.map do |order|
          {
            id: order[:id],
            unit: order[:unit],
            task: order[:task],
            labor_minutes: order[:labor_minutes]
          }
        end
      end

      private

      def require_open(id)
        order = fetch(id)
        raise ArgumentError, "work order #{id} is closed" unless order[:status] == "open"

        order
      end
    end
  end
end

module FleetDesk
  module Services
    # Shop-wide dashboard and per-vehicle history rollups.
    #
    # The shop dashboard is the hottest read in the app (the wall display
    # polls it), so it is memoized; write paths call #invalidate.
    class ReportService
      def initialize(orders, vehicles)
        @orders = orders
        @vehicles = vehicles
        @shop = nil
      end

      def shop_dashboard
        @shop ||= compute_shop
      end

      def invalidate
        @shop = nil
      end

      def unit_report(unit)
        vehicle = @vehicles.find(unit) or raise NotFound, "no vehicle with unit #{unit}"
        history = @orders.for_unit(unit)
        {
          unit: vehicle[:unit],
          desc: vehicle[:desc],
          mileage: vehicle[:mileage],
          orders: history.map { |o| { id: o[:id], task: o[:task], status: o[:status] } },
          labor_minutes: history.sum { |o| o[:labor_minutes] },
          parts_cents: history.sum { |o| o[:parts_cents] }
        }
      end

      private

      def compute_shop
        open = @orders.all.select { |order| order[:status] == "open" }
        {
          open_orders: open.length,
          labor_minutes: open.sum { |o| o[:labor_minutes] },
          parts_cents: open.sum { |o| o[:parts_cents] },
          units: open.map { |o| o[:unit] }.uniq.sort
        }
      end
    end
  end
end

      def initialize(orders, vehicles, reports)

        @vehicles = vehicles
        @reports = reports
      end

      def open_order(unit:, task:)
        raise NotFound, "no vehicle with unit #{unit}" unless @vehicles.exists?(unit)
        raise ArgumentError, "task must not be blank" if task.nil? || task.strip.empty?

        order = @orders.insert(

          status: "open",
          labor_minutes: 0,
          parts_cents: 0,
          labor_log: [],
          parts: []
        )

        order
      end

      def log_labor(id, minutes:, note: nil)
        order = require_open(id)
        unless minutes.is_a?(Integer) && minutes > 0
          raise ArgumentError, "minutes must be a positive integer"
        end

        order[:labor_minutes] += minutes
        order[:labor_log] << { minutes: minutes, note: note }
        @orders.update(order)
        order
      end

      def add_part(id, item:, cents:)
        order = require_open(id)
        raise ArgumentError, "item must not be blank" if item.nil? || item.strip.empty?
        unless cents.is_a?(Integer) && cents > 0
          raise ArgumentError, "cents must be a positive integer"
        end

        order[:parts_cents] += cents
        order[:parts] << { item: item, cents: cents }
        @orders.update(order)
        @reports.invalidate
        order
      end

      def close_order(id)
        order = require_open(id)
        order[:status] = "closed"
        @orders.update(order)
        @reports.invalidate
        order
      end

        @orders.find(id) or raise NotFound, "no such work order: #{id}"
      end

            id: order[:id],
            unit: order[:unit],
            task: order[:task],
            labor_minutes: order[:labor_minutes]
          }
        end
      end

      private

      def require_open(id)
        order = fetch(id)
        raise ArgumentError, "work order #{id} is closed" unless order[:status] == "open"

      end
    end
  end

Media-transcode ticket. Our thumbnail service feeds jobs to a pool of worker threads over channels, but the current code has two production bugs on file: (1) results come back in completion order, so page 3's thumbnails render into page 1's slots whenever a small image overtakes a big one, and (2) a panic inside one job takes down its worker and the collector waits forever on a channel that will never close — we hung a deploy for 40 minutes that way. Build the replacement: a proper mpsc fan-out/fan-in pipeline with submission-order reassembly and panics converted to a typed error.

This crate is rs-mpscpipe (lib name rs_mpscpipe, Cargo.toml already in place — leave it and .gitignore alone). Stdlib only (std::sync::mpsc, std::thread, std::panic). Everything in src/. The acceptance contract is tests/mpscpipe.rs, byte for byte as checked in: `cargo test --offline` fully green, test file untouched.

Public API, exactly this:

- `pub enum PipeError { ZeroWorkers, JobPanicked { index: u64, message: String } }` — derive Debug, PartialEq, Eq.
- `pub struct Pipeline<T, R>` for `T: Send + 'static, R: Send + 'static` with:
  - `pub fn new<F>(workers: usize, job_fn: F) -> Result<Self, PipeError> where F: Fn(u64, T) -> R + Send + Sync + 'static` — spawns exactly `workers` worker threads up front; `workers == 0` is `ZeroWorkers`. Workers pull jobs from one shared queue (competitive consumption) and fan results back over one mpsc channel.
  - `pub fn submit(&mut self, item: T) -> u64` — non-blocking; returns this job's submission index, counting from 0. The job_fn is invoked as `job_fn(index, item)`.
  - `pub fn finish(self) -> Result<Vec<R>, PipeError>` — closes the input, waits for every submitted job, joins ALL worker threads, and only then returns.

Semantics the tests pin down:

- finish() returns results in SUBMISSION order, index for index, no matter which worker finished first — the contract includes channel-gated tests where job 1 provably completes before job 0 (and a three-stage chain forcing completion order 2,1,0). Reassemble by index; do not trust arrival order.
- A panicking job must be caught inside the worker (std::panic::catch_unwind), the worker itself survives and keeps pulling jobs, and every other job still runs to completion. finish() then reports `JobPanicked { index, message }` for the LOWEST panicked submission index. Panic payloads: &str and String payloads become the message verbatim; anything else becomes exactly "<non-string panic>".
- finish() must never hang and never propagate a panic — one test drives it from a monitor thread with a 10s backstop, and the hang-on-panic bug above is exactly what it's checking.
- Clean shutdown: by the time finish() returns, all worker threads are joined and the job closure has been dropped (a test proves this by watching a Sender captured in the closure become Disconnected — that must hold on the error path too).
- Zero submissions: finish() is Ok(vec![]). T and R carry no Clone/Default bounds; values move through.

No public API beyond the above. No sleeps, no polling loops, no timeouts as synchronization anywhere in the implementation — channel disconnection and joins are all you need, and same input must behave identically on every run.

Media-transcode ticket. Our thumbnail service feeds jobs to a pool of worker threads over channels, but the current code has two production bugs on file: (1) results come back in completion order, so page 3's thumbnails render into page 1's slots whenever a small image overtakes a big one, and (2) a panic inside one job takes down its worker and the collector waits forever on a channel that will never close — we hung a deploy for 40 minutes that way. Build the replacement: a proper mpsc fan-out/fan-in pipeline with submission-order reassembly and panics converted to a typed error.

This crate is rs-mpscpipe (lib name rs_mpscpipe, Cargo.toml already in place — leave it and .gitignore alone). Stdlib only (std::sync::mpsc, std::thread, std::panic). Everything in src/. The acceptance contract is tests/mpscpipe.rs, byte for byte as checked in: `cargo test --offline` fully green, test file untouched.

Public API, exactly this:

- `pub enum PipeError { ZeroWorkers, JobPanicked { index: u64, message: String } }` — derive Debug, PartialEq, Eq.
- `pub struct Pipeline<T, R>` for `T: Send + 'static, R: Send + 'static` with:
  - `pub fn new<F>(workers: usize, job_fn: F) -> Result<Self, PipeError> where F: Fn(u64, T) -> R + Send + Sync + 'static` — spawns exactly `workers` worker threads up front; `workers == 0` is `ZeroWorkers`. Workers pull jobs from one shared queue (competitive consumption) and fan results back over one mpsc channel.
  - `pub fn submit(&mut self, item: T) -> u64` — non-blocking; returns this job's submission index, counting from 0. The job_fn is invoked as `job_fn(index, item)`.
  - `pub fn finish(self) -> Result<Vec<R>, PipeError>` — closes the input, waits for every submitted job, joins ALL worker threads, and only then returns.

Semantics the tests pin down:

- finish() returns results in SUBMISSION order, index for index, no matter which worker finished first — the contract includes channel-gated tests where job 1 provably completes before job 0 (and a three-stage chain forcing completion order 2,1,0). Reassemble by index; do not trust arrival order.
- A panicking job must be caught inside the worker (std::panic::catch_unwind), the worker itself survives and keeps pulling jobs, and every other job still runs to completion. finish() then reports `JobPanicked { index, message }` for the LOWEST panicked submission index. Panic payloads: &str and String payloads become the message verbatim; anything else becomes exactly "<non-string panic>".
- finish() must never hang and never propagate a panic — one test drives it from a monitor thread with a 10s backstop, and the hang-on-panic bug above is exactly what it's checking.
- Clean shutdown: by the time finish() returns, all worker threads are joined and the job closure has been dropped (a test proves this by watching a Sender captured in the closure become Disconnected — that must hold on the error path too).
- Zero submissions: finish() is Ok(vec![]). T and R carry no Clone/Default bounds; values move through.

No public API beyond the above. No sleeps, no polling loops, no timeouts as synchronization anywhere in the implementation — channel disconnection and joins are all you need, and same input must behave identically on every run.

Create `ini.h` and `ini.c` in this directory; the acceptance tests in `test_ini.c` build against them via `make test`.

```c
typedef struct {
    char *base;   /* caller-provided storage */
    size_t cap;   /* total bytes available */
    size_t used;  /* bytes handed out so far */
} ini_arena;

typedef struct {
    const char *section;  /* "" for pairs before the first [section] */
    const char *key;
    const char *value;
    size_t line;          /* 1-based line the pair appeared on */
} ini_pair;

enum {
    INI_OK       = 0,
    INI_EARG     = -1,   /* bad call arguments */
    INI_ESECTION = -2,   /* malformed [section] header */
    INI_EKEY     = -3,   /* missing '=' or empty key */
    INI_EQUOTE   = -4,   /* unterminated quote or unknown escape */
    INI_ETRAIL   = -5,   /* text after a closing quote */
    INI_ENOMEM   = -6    /* arena or pair table exhausted */
};

void ini_arena_init(ini_arena *a, void *storage, size_t cap);

               ini_pair *pairs, size_t max_pairs,
               size_t *err_line, size_t *err_col);
```

- Blank lines and full-line comments are skipped. A comment line is one whose first non-blank character is `;` or `#`. Those characters are NOT comment starters elsewhere: an unquoted value keeps any `;` or `#` inside it.
- `[name]` switches the current section. The name is trimmed of surrounding blanks and must be non-empty. The header may have blanks around it but nothing else on the line.
- `key = value` lines split at the FIRST `=`. Key and value are trimmed of surrounding blanks; the key must be non-empty, the value may be empty. Later `=` characters belong to the value. Duplicate keys are legal and every occurrence is appended in document order; the same section may be reopened.
- If the trimmed value starts with `"`, it is a quoted value: everything up to the matching close quote is taken verbatim (leading/trailing blanks inside are kept), with exactly four escapes decoded: `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`. - `INI_EQUOTE`: unterminated quoted value -> column of the opening quote; unknown escape -> column of the backslash.
- `INI_ETRAIL`: non-blank text after the closing quote -> column of that text.
- `INI_ENOMEM`: arena too small for the next string, or `pairs` already holds `max_pairs` entries when another pair shows up -> line of the offending pair, column 0.

Arena discipline: `ini_arena_init` just records the storage block and resets `used`; `ini_parse` bump-allocates from it and never frees. Text with no pairs at all (empty string, only comments/blanks) is a successful parse returning 0. The last line participates even without a trailing newline. The checkpoint package (job progress snapshots for our batch jobs) does its job in prod but is a wall for testing: os.MkdirAll/WriteFile/ReadDir/Remove and time.Now() are called inline all over, so the importer team tests it with real sleeps and a real spool dir, and that suite flaked twice last week on a slow runner. Production keeps working through shipped adapters: NewOSStore(dir) (creates the directory, lists/reads/writes/removes real files, skips subdirectories) and SystemClock{} for the wall clock. The old package-level Save/Latest/Resume/SweepStale go away — callers construct a Keeper now. ErrNoCheckpoint stays.

Nothing observable changes: same <job>-<10-digit-unix>.ckpt names (ops sorts these lexically, keep the zero padding), job parsed from the LAST hyphen so hyphenated job names keep working, newest-by-embedded-timestamp selection regardless of listing order, Resume treating age of exactly maxAge as still fresh and missing/stale as (nil, false, nil), SweepStale deleting strictly-older checkpoints across all jobs and returning removed names ascending while leaving non-checkpoint files alone. keeper_test.go is the contract — it drives everything with a scripted clock and an in-memory store and also exercises the OS adapters; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass without touching the test file.

We keep a family of initramfs and rescue-shell hook scripts that run before /usr is mounted. PATH is legitimately empty at that point, and every hook has grown its own broken trim/pad helper that forks out to sed or tr — which simply are not there that early. I want one library the hooks can all source: `strlib.sh` in the repo root, bash builtins and parameter expansion / brace expansion / printf -v only. If it forks, it is broken: the acceptance harness empties PATH before sourcing, so any external command dies loudly.

Ground rules:
- Sourcing the file defines the functions and does nothing else — no output, and sourcing it twice is harmless.
- Calling convention (printf -v style): every function's FIRST argument is the NAME of the destination variable; the remaining arguments are inputs. Callers use ordinary names like `s`, `out`, `result`, so prefix your internal locals (e.g. `__s`) or they will capture the destination and the result never reaches the caller.
- Everything runs under LC_ALL=C.

Functions, exact semantics:
- `str_trim DEST S`, `str_ltrim DEST S`, `str_rtrim DEST S` — strip whitespace (space, tab, CR, LF) from both ends / the left / the right. Interior whitespace is untouched.
- `str_pad_left DEST S WIDTH [PADCHAR]`, `str_pad_right DEST S WIDTH [PADCHAR]` — pad until the length is at least WIDTH. Pad char defaults to a space; only the FIRST character of PADCHAR is used. Never truncate: a string already at or past WIDTH comes back unchanged, and WIDTH < 1 is a no-op.
- `str_upper DEST S`, `str_lower DEST S` — ASCII case mapping (this is what ${S^^} / ${S,,} give you); under LC_ALL=C bytes outside ASCII pass through untouched.
- `str_replace_all DEST S NEEDLE REPLACEMENT` — replace every occurrence, scanning left to right, non-overlapping (aa -> b applied to "aaa" gives "ba"). NEEDLE is LITERAL text: *, ?, [ab] in a needle match only themselves, never as globs — mind how you quote the pattern expansion. An empty NEEDLE returns S unchanged.
- `str_basename DEST PATH`, `str_dirname DEST PATH` — clones of basename(1)/dirname(1) built from ${var##*/} / ${var%/*} logic. Edge tables, exactly:

    basename: a/b/c -> c | a/b/c/ -> c | a//b// -> b | c -> c | /x -> x | / -> / | /// -> / | (empty) -> .
    dirname:  a/b/c -> a/b | a/b/c/// -> a/b | a/b/ -> a | a//b//c -> a//b (interior doubled slashes are kept) | c -> . | /x -> / | / -> / | /// -> / | (empty) -> .

Acceptance: `bash test_strlib.sh` from the workspace root must pass unmodified. Do not modify the test file.

The sample accumulator in `src/accumulate.S` returns plausible values in its leaf-style smoke test, but the instrumented C callback reports an invalid stack boundary. Builds whose callback spills aligned vector data can fail outright. Repair the assembly helper at the ABI boundary without changing its public API or the callback contract.

`accumulate_samples(const long *samples, size_t count, long bias)` must call `abi_transform(sample, index, bias)` exactly once for every element, in ascending index order, and return the sum of those callback return values. The callback deliberately destroys caller-saved integer registers, so loop state that survives the call must remain in ABI-safe storage.

Keep the existing frame unwindable. Its DWARF CFI must continue to describe the canonical frame and every saved nonvolatile register across the nested call; do not trade stack alignment for inaccurate unwind metadata. Make the smallest root-cause repair in `src/accumulate.S`. Do not modify the protected ABI fixture, C tests, unwind checker, header, or build files, and do not bypass or replace the callback. Our audit-log export endpoint streams NDJSON over chunked HTTP/1.1 — chunkstream.ts writes straight to the connection so we never buffer a whole export. Two kinds of tickets since the compliance dashboards moved onto it, and I've stared at this code way too long.

One: some exports just stop partway. The download 'completes' as far as curl is concerned, but the last chunk of records is missing. It's always the SAME exports that truncate — retries change nothing — while both tiny and huge exports are usually fine, so it isn't a size cap or a timeout. Diffing two exports that differ by one record: one is complete, the other loses everything after a certain line. Cannot see a pattern.

Two: when the upstream log reader errors mid-export, our API docs promise the client gets a trailing {"error": ...} record and a clean end of body. What clients actually see is literal 'HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error' text spliced INTO the middle of the download, and strict clients then scream about malformed chunked encoding. When the reader errors before any output, though, the 500 comes out perfectly — which makes even less sense to me.

A teammate turned captured connection bytes into test_stream.ts using a fake socket, so the whole mess reproduces deterministically: node --test test_stream.ts fails today exactly the way production does (and it re-checks the exports that DO work, which must keep working). Find what's wrong in chunkstream.ts and fix it; the test file is read-only, and don't 'fix' it by buffering whole exports in memory — streaming stays.

TASK
Warehouse ops lives in TSV exports and every enrichment step is somebody's fragile one-off pipeline. I want the join step done once, properly: `tsvjoin.sh` in the repo root, plain bash around the classic sort/join/awk toolbox, portable flags only. Our exports are strict TSV: first line is the header (tab-separated column names), fields never contain tabs or newlines and are never empty.

Usage: `tsvjoin.sh [--key NAME] <left.tsv> <right.tsv>`. The key column is selected by NAME and may sit at a different position in each file; with no --key, the left file's first column name is the key. It's a LEFT join: every left data row appears in the output exactly as many times as it has right-side matches, and at least once — rows with no match get a literal `-` in each right-side output column. If the right file has several rows with the same key, the left row repeats once per match, standard join semantics.

Output to stdout, byte-exact: first the joined header — all left columns in their original order, then the right file's columns in their original order minus the key column — then the body. Body order must be deterministic, diff-stable run to run: rows ascending by key in plain C byte order (pin LC_ALL=C inside the script); among rows with equal keys, the contributing left rows in their C-sorted whole-line order, and for each left row its right matches in their C-sorted whole-line order. That's exactly what you get from stripping the headers, `LC_ALL=C sort`-ing each body on the key column, joining, and re-attaching the fresh header — headers must never be sorted into the data.

Edge behavior, all of which I hit weekly: a header-only right file (fresh catalog) means every left row comes out `-`-filled; a header-only left file means the output is just the joined header; both header-only, same. A zero-byte file has no header and is an error: `tsvjoin.sh: empty file: <arg>` on stderr, exit 65, left file checked before right. A key name that isn't in a file's header: `tsvjoin.sh: no such column: <NAME> in <arg>` on stderr, exit 65, again left first. Missing/unreadable file: `tsvjoin.sh: cannot read: <arg>`, exit 66, checked before the empty-file check. Bad invocation (not exactly two files, unknown flag, --key with no value): `usage: tsvjoin.sh [--key NAME] <left.tsv> <right.tsv>` on stderr, exit 64. Success: exit 0, stderr silent.

trap cleanup EXIT

Usage: `tsvjoin.sh [--key NAME] <left.tsv> <right.tsv>`. The key column is selected by NAME and may sit at a different position in each file; with no --key, the left file's first column name is the key. It's a LEFT join: every left data row appears in the output exactly as many times as it has right-side matches, and at least once — rows with no match get a literal `-` in each right-side output column. Warehouse ops lives in TSV exports and every enrichment step is somebody's fragile one-off pipeline. I want the join step done once, properly: `tsvjoin.sh` in the repo root, plain bash around the classic sort/join/awk toolbox, portable flags only. Our exports are strict TSV: first line is the header (tab-separated column names), fields never contain tabs or newlines and are never empty.

Usage: `tsvjoin.sh [--key NAME] <left.tsv> <right.tsv>`. The key column is selected by NAME and may sit at a different position in each file; with no --key, the left file's first column name is the key. It's a LEFT join: every left data row appears in the output exactly as many times as it has right-side matches, and at least once — rows with no match get a literal `-` in each right-side output column. If the right file has several rows with the same key, the left row repeats once per match, standard join semantics.

Output to stdout, byte-exact: first the joined header — all left columns in their original order, then the right file's columns in their original order minus the key column — then the body. Body order must be deterministic, diff-stable run to run: rows ascending by key in plain C byte order (pin LC_ALL=C inside the script); among rows with equal keys, the contributing left rows in their C-sorted whole-line order, and for each left row its right matches in their C-sorted whole-line order. That's exactly what you get from stripping the headers, `LC_ALL=C sort`-ing each body on the key column, joining, and re-attaching the fresh header — headers must never be sorted into the data.

Edge behavior, all of which I hit weekly: a header-only right file (fresh catalog) means every left row comes out `-`-filled; a header-only left file means the output is just the joined header; both header-only, same. A zero-byte file has no header and is an error: `tsvjoin.sh: empty file: <arg>` on stderr, exit 65, left file checked before right. A key name that isn't in a file's header: `tsvjoin.sh: no such column: <NAME> in <arg>` on stderr, exit 65, again left first. Missing/unreadable file: `tsvjoin.sh: cannot read: <arg>`, exit 66, checked before the empty-file check. Bad invocation (not exactly two files, unknown flag, --key with no value): `usage: tsvjoin.sh [--key NAME] <left.tsv> <right.tsv>` on stderr, exit 64. Success: exit 0, stderr silent.

`bash test_tsvjoin.sh` from the workspace root is the acceptance gate; it must pass unmodified — don't touch the test file.

Warehouse ops lives in TSV exports and every enrichment step is somebody's fragile one-off pipeline. I want the join step done once, properly: `tsvjoin.sh` in the repo root, plain bash around the classic sort/join/awk toolbox, portable flags only. Our exports are strict TSV: first line is the header (tab-separated column names), fields never contain tabs or newlines and are never empty.

Usage: `tsvjoin.sh [--key NAME] <left.tsv> <right.tsv>`. The key column is selected by NAME and may sit at a different position in each file; with no --key, the left file's first column name is the key. It's a LEFT join: every left data row appears in the output exactly as many times as it has right-side matches, and at least once — rows with no match get a literal `-` in each right-side output column. If the right file has several rows with the same key, the left row repeats once per match, standard join semantics.

Output to stdout, byte-exact: first the joined header — all left columns in their original order, then the right file's columns in their original order minus the key column — then the body. Body order must be deterministic, diff-stable run to run: rows ascending by key in plain C byte order (pin LC_ALL=C inside the script); among rows with equal keys, the contributing left rows in their C-sorted whole-line order, and for each left row its right matches in their C-sorted whole-line order. That's exactly what you get from stripping the headers, `LC_ALL=C sort`-ing each body on the key column, joining, and re-attaching the fresh header — headers must never be sorted into the data.

Edge behavior, all of which I hit weekly: a header-only right file (fresh catalog) means every left row comes out `-`-filled; a header-only left file means the output is just the joined header; both header-only, same. A zero-byte file has no header and is an error: `tsvjoin.sh: empty file: <arg>` on stderr, exit 65, left file checked before right. A key name that isn't in a file's header: `tsvjoin.sh: no such column: <NAME> in <arg>` on stderr, exit 65, again left first. One-minute repro in a scratch checkout: create the usual fixture dirs (a couple of non-empty files under src/, a couple of .sql files under migrations/), truncate one of the src files to zero bytes, then run `bash rollout.sh`. I want a tiny per-directory maintenance log driven by one bash script, `maintlog.sh`, in the repo root. Plain bash, and do it the bash way: short options parsed with getopts in silent mode (leading colon — we control every error message ourselves), and the common long spellings accepted by rewriting them to the short form before getopts runs.

Storage: `.maintlog` in the current directory, one entry per line, tab-separated fields: seq, host, tag, message. seq starts at 1 and increments per entry. Fields never contain tabs — reject any add that would break that.

Commands:
- `init` — create an empty `.maintlog` here. stdout: `initialized .maintlog`. If the file already exists: stderr `maintlog: already initialized`, exit 65.
- `add -H <host> -m <text> [-t <tag>]` — append an entry; tag defaults to `-`. stdout: `added #<seq>`. Run before init: stderr `maintlog: not initialized (run 'maintlog.sh init' first)`, exit 65 (this check comes before option parsing). Missing OR empty -H/-m: `maintlog: add: -H and -m are required` + usage, exit 64. Any field containing a tab: `maintlog: fields may not contain tabs`, exit 65.
- `report [-H <host>] [-n <count>]` — print matching entries oldest first, each as `#<seq>` then host, tag, message, tab-separated (i.e. `#` + the stored line). -H filters by exact host match. -n keeps only the last <count> entries of the filtered set (a count larger than the log just means everything). count must be a positive decimal integer; anything else is `maintlog: invalid count: <value>` + usage, exit 64. Before init: same 65 as add. No matches is fine: print nothing, exit 0.

Long options: accept `--host=<v>`, `--message=<v>`, `--tag=<v>`, `--limit=<v>`, `--help` by translating to -H/-m/-t/-n/-h ahead of getopts. Any other argument starting with `--` is `maintlog: unknown option: <arg>` + usage, exit 64. Known limitation I am fine with: the rewrite pass looks at every argument after the command word, so option VALUES must not themselves start with `--` (use the short option for those).

Exit-code contract: 0 ok, 64 usage error, 65 data error. Usage errors print their one-line message and then the usage block, both to stderr. Data errors print only their one-line message to stderr. `-h` or `--help` in place of a command, or `-h` after add/report, prints the usage block to stdout and exits 0. No command at all: `maintlog: missing command` + usage, 64. Unknown command word: `maintlog: unknown command: <word>` + usage, 64. Unknown short option: `maintlog: unknown option: -<x>` + usage, 64. A short option missing its value: `maintlog: option -<x> requires a value` + usage, 64. Trailing non-option junk after add/report options: `maintlog: <command>: unexpected argument: <word>` + usage, 64.

usage: maintlog.sh <command> [options]

commands:
  init                                  create an empty log in this directory
  add -H <host> -m <text> [-t <tag>]    append a maintenance entry
  report [-H <host>] [-n <count>]       print entries, oldest first

long options: --host=<v>  --message=<v>  --tag=<v>  --limit=<v>  --help
exit codes:   0 ok, 64 usage error, 65 data error

Need a health-check orchestrator for the deploy gate service. We have one, but it's welded to real setTimeout so the test suite takes four minutes and still flakes; this rewrite must take ALL timing through an injected scheduler. TypeScript, no dependencies, one file healthgate.ts exporting class HealthGate.

constructor({ scheduler, flapThreshold = 1, timeoutMs = 5000 }). scheduler is { setTimeout(fn, delayMs) -> id, clearTimeout(id) } — the orchestrator must never call the global timers, and it must clean up after itself: when a check settles before its deadline the timeout gets cleared, so a fake scheduler shows zero pending timers after a round.

add({ name, run, after?, critical?, timeoutMs?, retries?, retryDelayMs? }) registers a check. run is an async function: resolve = pass, reject = fail (reason from the error message; a synchronous throw counts the same). Duplicate names are an error naming the name.

runRound() executes every check once and resolves to { results, overall }:
- Order: checks run one at a time, in dependency order — `after` lists the checks that must run first. Ties (several ready at once) break by registration order. An `after` naming an unregistered check rejects with unknown dependency, quoting both names; cycles reject with a message containing "cycle".
- Each attempt races run() against timeoutMs on the scheduler; hitting the deadline fails the attempt with reason "timeout", and anything the check does after that is ignored. On failure the check retries up to `retries` more times, waiting retryDelayMs between attempts (0 = immediately, no timer). results entries are { name, result: pass|fail|skipped, reason (null on pass), attempts }.
- If a dependency's result this round is fail or skipped, the dependent does NOT run: result skipped, attempts 0, reason naming the first such dependency from its `after` list, and this cascades.
- Flap damping: each check keeps a damped "reported" state. The first observed result is adopted outright; after that it takes flapThreshold consecutive contrary rounds to flip, an agreeing round resets the streak, and skipped rounds neither count nor reset. results always show the raw round outcome; `overall` and status() use the damped states.
- overall: down if any critical check's reported state is fail; degraded if any non-critical one is; healthy otherwise. Skipped/never-run checks stay out of the aggregate.

status() -> { overall, checks } from the damped states at any time; before any round it's healthy with an empty map.

Acceptance: test_healthgate.ts (protected), run `node --test test_healthgate.ts`. The suite drives a fake scheduler and scripted checks — read it for the exact semantics of every corner.
